In modern cloud data centers, the surge in user requests necessitates a robust method for managing virtual machine (VM) workflows to ensure efficient service. However, uneven load distribution can degrade both performance and user satisfaction by causing over-provisioning in some areas and under-provisioning in others. Consequently, load distribution is a critical operational challenge. This paper introduces a novel preemptive strategy designed to balance the workload across VMs, enhancing the effectiveness of pre-assignment scheduling. Operating on a pre-assignment framework where resources are allocated based on user requests upon arrival, our approach mitigates unnecessary delays and reduces the risk of resource conflicts. By avoiding the "free-riding" behavior of users who might delay submitting requests to secure lower costs, the method encourages timely submission to improve overall system utilization. Experimental results confirm that the strategy is efficient, scalable, robust to parameter variations, and robustly reliable.

This work examines novel, model-free upper limits on the causal average treatment effect, introducing an assessment procedure that does not rely on specific parametric assumptions. The efficacy of these limits hinges on the availability of treated and control units with quantities that allow for robust comparison. Consequently, an algorithm is developed to identify a specific subset of control units that produces the tightest possible upper bound. The causal impacts limit then emerges by evaluating the performance of the chosen region across the spectrum of all potential outcomes. The test method employs a combination of convex programming and optimization strategies. The framework is designed to be versatile, accommodating various influence mechanisms, varying sample sizes, and data in many dimensions. The investigation begins by exploring how these restrictions behave when applied uniformly across entire populations versus when targeted at specific subgroups. Subsequently, the methodology is extended to handle high-dimensional information, utilizing techniques such as sparsity constraints and dimension reduction. The efficiency and precision of the algorithm are demonstrated through numerical simulations and real-world applications.

This work addresses a critical challenge in security-critical systems: protecting a system from attacks by ensuring that the future output prediction error remains below a specified limit despite potential vulnerabilities inherent in the system and protective mechanisms. To this end, we propose a control strategy featuring a feedback loop where the input is adjusted based on prediction error, enabling a security analysis that mirrors that of standard predictive control methods. We derive precise conditions for a security threshold, demonstrating that even with conservative uncertainty bounds, prediction error remains within limits. We also establish conditions for robust stability, ensuring that states remain within bounded, predictable ranges. Additionally, we present operational conditions for achieving arbitrary performance and asymptotic stability, ensuring that the prediction error can be made arbitrarily small. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings using a power network case study, and make our Open-source Python tool available at https://github.com/ruanwang/e-SEP-control for community use.

Document summarization is a critical component of information retrieval, and while significant advancements have been made in English, progress in Indian languages has remained limited. This study presents a language-agnostic approach for extracting unmonitored summaries, grounded in the assumption that related documents share similar lexical and structural traits. By generating word embeddings and establishing a mapping between them, the proposed framework constructs corresponding embeddings for the sentence-level syntax trees. Subsequently, graph similarity measures are utilized to evaluate these tree representations. Experimental results across both English and Indian languages demonstrate that this unmonitored approach yields state-of-the-art performance, underscoring its viability and applicability.

This paper addresses the structure of Noether subrings and introduces an analog of Noether modules specifically for s-subrings, defining them as "s-rings of Noether type." Functions as central to this structure are the star ideals (internal stars), and an s-ring $S$ qualifies as being of Noether type if all its internal stars form a Noether module over $S$. We demonstrate that any finitarily modular subring of noether type adheres to the second ascending condition regarding their s-ideals and satisfies huppert's principle. Additionally, we formulate a variant of quenelle's theorem.

This study investigates astrometric data from five accelerating stars—HD 114762, HD 142529, HD 191569, HD 196558, and TYC 2106-188- 1—to refine the constraints on the masses and distances of their unseen companion objects. By applying a Markov Chain Monte Carlo analysis, we simultaneously fit the single-liner models from Gaia DR2 and EDR3 against Gaia DR3 astrometry, alongside proper motion and parallax data from DR4 EDR3 and DR5 EDR3, respectively. This holistic approach yields more robust estimates of mass and distance for the hidden companions than previous analyses based on individual datasets. Notably, the inferred distances to these systems are significantly closer to those predicted by mass function studies. Additionally, by eliminating prior distance assumptions, we have updated the mass distributions for hidden populations around the five target stars.

Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) have become a foundational tool in machine learning, particularly for unsupervised representation learning and generative modeling. Their appeal stems from their generative capabilities and the ability to maintain an efficient, lower-dimensional data encoding. However, the standard VAE model can suffer from issues including poor reconstruction, underparameterization, and overparameterization. To address these drawbacks, this research introduces a Variational Bayes Autoencoder with Regularized constraints (VBAE-Reg), designed to outperform traditional VAEs. Extensive experimental validation across diverse datasets demonstrates that the proposed model consistently surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches in terms of both underparameterization and recovery of lost information.

As a private blockchain innovation, EVOCHAIN serves to secure this data and mitigate the risks of unauthorized access. Equipped with localized IoT sensors and AI, the system detects and identifies unusual activity patterns to protect users against both physical and digital threats. By integrating blockchain for decentralized, tamper-proof storage of data, the solution ensures secure and efficient processing. The framework is further fortified by a Machine Learning-based authentication mechanism that prevents unauthorized device usage.

Quantifying channel loss parameters ($L$ values) is essential for modern communication systems. In this context, we present a method to reduce the bit resolution of $L$ values while maintaining performance. Conventional quantization relies on uniform spacing; our approach utilizes a deep neural network to optimize the distribution of quantized levels specifically tailored to maintain error performance. Initially, however, level distribution is approximated via the Probability Density Function (PDF) of $L$ values. A common assumption treats the PDF as independent of transmission conditions. Our analysis reveals that such PDF dependence varies across scenarios, particularly when channel estimation errors exist. Furthermore, we evaluate the impact of introducing feedback information regarding the channel condition on quantization efficiency. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that the proposed dynamic quantization scheme effectively enhances $L$ value handling accuracy under quantized constraints, even when accounting for estimation errors and state feedback.

Crowdsourcing has emerged as a widely adopted method for generating large datasets for machine learning, though incorporating human-generated information often results in higher entropy compared to data derived from automated sources. To exemplify this, we utilize the widely recognized Caltech-UBECT (Caltech-UNED) dataset, which features hand-written textual annotations. These textual descriptions were noisily produced by humans and suffer from inconsistency. To mitigate these issues, we present an ensemble modeling approach that utilizes "human softmax" distributions to capture the variability of noisy annotations. By incorporating human factors such as inconsistency and ambiguity, the proposed framework aims to improve classification accuracy and reduce uncertainty in predictions. Evaluation results indicate that employing human softmax distributions outperforms traditional averaging methods in dealing with noisy annotations. Furthermore, we analyze uncertainty metrics to quantify the degree of inconsistency in human labeling.

We demonstrate that for non-autonomous dynamical systems exhibiting uniform hyperbolicity and the uniform normal derivative property, accompanied by a sufficient rate of dynamical stability, there exists a unique invariant measure. Minor strength-2 covering arrays (mSCAs) are defined as a variant of conventional covering arrays that allow a specified set of subsets within index sets to function as subsets, thereby linking them closely to classical covering array theory and maintaining a simpler structure. This work focuses on the algorithmic aspects of constructing MSCAs, specifically analyzing classes of minimal MSCAs and tight MSCAs. We present algorithms capable of generating these array types and compare their computational performance against established heuristics for standard covering array construction. Furthermore, we examine fundamental problems related to building MSCAs, including a time-complexity analysis of the algorithm proposed. Finally, this research establishes the connections between MSCAs and classical covering array theory, highlighting areas for future research in both theoretical and practical directions.

In high-$T_c$ cuprate superconductors, the vortex lattice is established through melting transitions, and both numerical simulations and theoretical frameworks have linked these events to fluctuations in vortex lattice order. However, experimental verification of this connection has remained elusive. This study introduces experimental evidence derived from radio-frequency SQUID on a chip measurements of YBCO films. These data reveal that during the melting process, fluctuations persist with square symmetry despite lacking a distinct lattice structure. Furthermore, exposure to an applied magnetic field aligns notches consistently in specific orientations relative to the lattice axes. Complementing this, vortex imaging via transmission electron microscopy (TEM) confirms the presence of a square symmetry grid in the vortex arrangement. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that vortex lattice order fluctuations indeed play a pivotal role in the melting phenomenon. Notably, the square symmetry of the fluctuations suggests the enduring influence of short-range correlations inherent in the vortex grid even upon approach to the melting point. Additionally, TEM observations indicate a critical magnetic field threshold below which a square symmetry grid emerges spontaneously within the lattice.

Our rigorous analysis shows these criteria closely align with findings derived from spin ice theory via the Linear Response Theory, thereby offering a robust framework to study magnetic ordering in these specific materials. Our approach is versatile, applicable not just to models with two-spin interactions but also to various extensions utilizing higher-spin interactions.

This paper addresses a critical and prevalent issue in biomedical research: identifying causal treatment effects following an initial intervention within a staged experimental design. We focus on scenarios where a screening phase precedes a second phase, which involves determining specific treatments for a subset of individuals who received the initial intervention. A key challenge in applying these second-stage methods is controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) effectively, as an excessive number of false positive findings can render large-scale studies useless. We propose a novel, data-driven procedure for regulating FDR that is capable of handling a vast quantity of hypothesis tests while accounting for dependence among them. This method is adaptable to various dependence structures and exhibits strong performance even when the quantity of hypothesis tests grows substantially. We also present an extensive simulation study that demonstrates the method's effectiveness and capacity for maintaining FDR control while achieving high statistical power. Finally, we apply the proposed approach to analyze results from a clinical trial involving the administration of remdesivir and hydroxychloroquine to COVID-19 patients.

While existing research confirms that conversational mutual synchronization enhances interaction quality, quantifying this synchronization remains difficult. This challenge stems from the inherent complexities of alignment processes—such as their distributed nature, dynamic variability, and the stochastic characteristics of the speech production pipeline. Addressing this gap, this paper introduces the initial application of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) to unsupervisedly synchronize and detect dialogue turns in spoken dialogues. We propose the Recurrent Neural Network of Neural Gabor Filters (RNN-GF), a deep architecture designed to extract speech features and align utterances within the same turn. Through a novel loss function, RNN-GF is trained to maximize the timing gap between turn boundaries, thereby serving as a robust unsupervised synchronization metric. Evaluated on the CHILL corpus, the model achieves an average absolute synchronization error of 45.8 ms and a mutual synchronization accuracy (Mutual AP) of 73.8%. We also investigate the correlation between the learned synchronization distances and actual turn alignment, with a particular focus on the impact of voice activity detection (VAD) errors.

Temporal action segmentation (TAS) aims to fragment video content into distinct functional segments. However, creating large-scale action datasets is costly and labor-intensive, prompting advancements in unsupervised TAS to eliminate the necessity for manual labeling. While some prior methods leverage co-occurrence relations to break videos into atomic parts and then ascend to higher-level segments, they often fail to capture functional hierarchy effectively. In response, we introduce Self-supervised Co-occurrence Action Parsing (SSCAP), a novel unsupervised framework that first decomposes video into co-occurring atomic elements and then utilizes a hierarchical self-supervised mechanism to refine segment boundaries. Additionally, we release SLCAP—a comprehensive novel dataset featuring hierarchical annotations. Our experimental results demonstrate that SSCAP significantly outperforms existing unsupervised and semi-supervised approaches on APTES-10 and DAS datasets, achieving mean average precision (MAP) scores of 20.6% and 26.9%, respectively.

We introduce two specialized neural network architectures designed to detect particle-object interactions in particle detectors. Both models incorporate domain-specific features aimed at enhancing representation learning for these roles. The first utilizes an end-to-end neural network, while the second employs a classical convolutional network augmented with a ZF region-based object detection architecture to extract region-specific features. Our findings indicate that the domain-specific network not only outperforms the standard ZF architecture but also surpasses many existing detectors. Furthermore, the purely domain-specific model matches the performance of ResNet50, all while requiring significantly less training data.

Atmospheres of extrasolar planets, moons, and stellar companions exist in conditions that are either too hot, high-pressure, or rich in molecular complexity for current models to handle efficiently. While models have been developed for individual conditions, a robust framework incorporating all such variables is still absent. Consequently, researchers are forced to re-run time-intensive quantum chemical calculations for every new study, even when using nearly identical but unmodeled conditions. To resolve this, we propose a new approach: the pre-computation of average, or effective, absorption spectra. By averaging over specific ranges of these varying parameters, we can significantly reduce computation times without sacrificing accuracy within those bounds. In this study, we introduce the Molecular Absorption Cross-Section Repository for Brown Dwarf and Exoplanet Line Emissions (EXOPLINES), a database containing average 2D effective spectra. These specific "effect" spectra are generated by varying both temperature and sub-stellar pressure. Each spectrum is further characterized by average pressure and maximum probing pressure values, which account for light scattering effects and aerosol presence. Accessible via exoplanlines.org alongside retrieval tools and relevant research, this repository facilitates rapid, precise radiative-convective equilibrium modeling of planets and stars.

This study investigates how disorder impacts two-dimensional higher-order topological insulators (HOTIs) by employing a mass-term approach grounded in the second-order perturbation of the tight-binding model. The resulting expressions for mass depend on the correlation functions of the underlying HOTIs' edge and surface states, respectively. The theoretical framework derived is subsequently employed to analyze the dynamics of surface localized electrons within a two-step lattice model as they respond to both weak and strong disorder regimes.

Magnetic reconnection is widely accepted as a primary mechanism for energy release in the solar corona, though its precise role in driving coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and associated coronal loops remains debated. The radio emission originates from plasma at temperatures exceeding 10 million Kelvin, allowing us to precisely track the rapid movement of the loop's leading edge. Our analysis indicates that the loop's motion aligns with models where a CME-driven shock wave propagates through the low corona, compressing loops rather than the loop expanding. Furthermore, radio data revealed an increase in plasma density by a factor of approximately 3.5 in the piston region compared to the quiescent loop, alongside strong indications of turbulent mixing. This level of mixing could facilitate the redistribution of non-thermal particles, potentially explaining the high flux observed in solar radio bursts.

Living organisms exhibit complex behaviors driven by interactions across multiple biological systems. To understand these living systems, time is a critical factor, and there is a growing demand for tools that can capture temporal dynamics within living cells. Current approaches for automated temporal analysis are hindered by their dependence on human expertise, high costs, and limited flexibility. Addressing this, the authors propose an artificial intelligence (AI)-based deep learning framework designed for the automated analysis of temporal life science data, which eliminates the need for time-based user guidance. Instead, the model autonomously learns temporal sequences by integrating them into a dedicated memory module. This self-supervised mechanism enhances flexibility when processing temporal data and improves accuracy, particularly with scarce training examples. This approach was evaluated using two distinct datasets: the first involves temporal sequences of animal behaviors from ethological studies, and the second involves temporal sequences of cell cycle stages in biology. The second dataset was further expanded by analyzing a large collection of cell cycle stage images (over 10,000 images) to capture temporal details. Results indicate the model's high performance, even with minimal data, and its capacity to manage detailed temporal datasets effectively. Furthermore, the model was applied to design experiments for generating synthetic temporal life cycle data, demonstrating its utility in creating realistic datasets. Ultimately, the proposed memory module is expected to advance future research and automated analysis of temporal life science data.

This paper investigates the utility of memory-augmented networks for making decisions and acquiring knowledge in partially observable settings. We focus on multi-step partially observable Markov decision processes ( POMDPs ), where agents must account for time, identify their current situation, and adapt their strategies based on what they understand about their environment. To address these challenges, we introduce two reinforcement learning algorithms—CB-MAP and CB-Q—designed to track an agent's beliefs regarding their environment and integrate this information into the decision-making process. We analyze the structural components of these algorithms, outline their theorems, and describe their operational mechanisms. We also explore specific network architectures used to implement the belief formation and decision-making components. The performance of these algorithms is evaluated across various well-established POMDP test cases.

Action detection relies heavily on the quality of its guidance, a factor often compromised by human annotation inconsistencies such as imprecise boundaries or incomplete key parts. This AIM functions alongside GCN to enhance the utilization of spatial-tempual information within the context of Grouph Convolutional Networks (GCN). Action localization experiments confirm the efficacy of these proposed methods.

Relying on a server, federated learning (FL) coordinates distributed clients to train a shared model. Since FL is designed for distributed environments, distributed, it necessitates a server-centric communication paradigm. This setup presents significant challenges regarding communication efficiency and privacy. In response, we introduce DP-REC, a new federated training algorithm that merges differential privacy (DP) with a recursive encoder (REC) strategy. DP-REC operates by having each client encode local data using a private, randomized, and stateful encoder, transmitting only the encoded outputs to the server for model updates. The integration of DP ensures the privacy of both local data and clients' encoded messages, while the stateful nature of REC enhances the quality of these transmissions. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that DP-CONVENIENCER achieves the same convergence rate as standard stochastic gradient descent (SGD) despite the added complexity and privacy constraints. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the method is robust against a malicious server, and experimental results on image classification tasks (MNIST and CIFAR-10) reveal that the approach offers strong protection for clients' private data while maintaining high communication efficiency.

This study presents far-ultraviolet (FUV) observations of young stellar objects (YSOs) within the Taurus, Perseus, and Auriga molecular clouds, utilizing FUV spectrographs aboard the *Hubble Space Telescope* and imaging modes from the *Galex* mission. The FUV spectra allow for the analysis of emission lines from neutral helium and ionized helium I and II, as well as C II, C III, C IV, N II, N III, O II, O III, and O I. FUV imaging data reveal that FUV radiation extends several hundred astronomical units (au) from Ysos, illuminating a comparable volume where photodissociation regions (PDRs) form. These regions are characterized by emission from the aforementioned lines and molecular bands, including the CO fundamental band. Additionally, *Galex* FUV imaging indicates that photodissociation regions extend significantly further, reaching several thousand astronomical units. These findings demonstrate that photoevaporation by FUV photons is a critical mechanism in the evolution of molecular clouds.

Tables embedded in PDF files offer a structured representation of information, offering significant potential to enhance document search capabilities. This work outlines the development of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) tailored for table extraction specifically. The primary challenge lies in accurately selecting table cells relevant to an input query and extracting their associated data. To address this, we designed a GNN-based representation encoding scheme that effectively captures the structural relationships between table cells and their queries. Our experimental results indicate that the proposed extraction representation scoring out traditional methods by a large margin.

This paper addresses a specific type of multi-phase game characterized by insufficient information, an framework established by Rubinstein and Peled. Within this context, players operate under only partial knowledge regarding future phases, forcing them to evaluate future actions based on their beliefs about what counterparts might do. To formalize these beliefs, we introduce an infinite hierarchy of cognitive layers. Each layer represents a distinct level of reasoning: a player at a given height is modeled as a best responder to their expected beliefs regarding the cognitive layers of their opponents. We further define two key properties for games: self-confirming equilibrium and weak self-confirming equilibrium. The former assumes players can forecast, with certainty, how their opponents will respond to the strategic environment (including equilibrium strategies) without error about specific equilibrium components. The latter is more permissive, tolerant that players have mistaken beliefs only about how their own strategies are perceived by opponents. The central contribution of our work is a representation that builds up from basic self-confirming equilibrium components to general, higher-order strategies. Specifically, we represent the strategies of players occupying finite cognitive layers as best responses to mixed strategies of their opponents, where the opponents' strategies are themselves drawn from the base set of self-confirming equilibrium profiles. Finally, we prove that the strategy sets generated by both types of players—those at finite cognitive layers and those at infinity—precisely and exhaustively cover the strategy space of the original game.

Accurate and timely population estimates are vital for the long-term sustainability of public service delivery in low- and middle-income nations. To achieve this, these countries must leverage their own human capital by training local professionals to manage survey operations, a necessity that is also critical for data quality assurance. This requirement is further underscored by high staff turnover and brain drain prevalent in regions like Mozambique. Consequently, an educational package was developed to empower human resources in Mozambique to independently manage the entire data collection phase of surveys, from start to finish. Through four field tests—three executed fully by local teams and one as the standard reference frame—the study evaluated the performance of this self-contained model. The results indicate that surveys managed entirely by local teams performed on par with the reference collection, yielding equivalent quality metrics across all dimensions. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that population censuses and household surveys in Mozambique can be successfully handled by indigenous teams without external involvement, thereby ensuring sustained survey operations.

The study presents an enhanced Smooth Particle Particle Hybrid (SPH) model featuring a multi-scale architecture to enhance computational efficiency. This framework integrates the Strongly Coupled Multi-Scale (SCMS) model with Smooth Particle Finite Element (SPFE) formulations. Within this approach, fluid dynamics are governed by a compressible equation of state utilizing the Modified Incompressible Fluid (MIF) model, while structural elements utilize SPFE elements augmented with artificial damping to simulate physical friction. The core SCMS structure enables the synchronization of structural and non-structural nodes at a coarser temporal resolution, thereby lowering computational burdens in fluid-structure interaction (FSI) simulations. To validate the SCMS-SPE fe framework, several representative cases were analyzed: a static bending test under distributed load, a free surface scenario with a free-falling tank, and a dynamic FSI simulation involving a flexible membrane exposed to oscillatory airflow. The results demonstrate that the SCMS-SPE fe model is a robust and efficient methodology for simulating complex multi-physical FSI challenges.

We introduce the Quantum Unmonitored Learning (QUL) algorithm, designed for use in Hilbert space and functioning similarly to kernel ridge regression but within quantum conditions. By drawing a comparison to classical kernel ridge regression, we demonstrate through quality-control analysis that QUL achieves performance comparable to its classical counterpart. We also present the instruct Quantum Learning (IQL) algorithm, which incorporates environmental noise into quantum learning. IQL extends the QUL framework by determining optimal parameters to maximize expected utility, a capability we verify using a two-qubit, two-class pattern recognition task. Both algorithms were executed and tested on Google's C6 superconducting superprocess. The results indicate that despite measurement errors, classical noise, and limited qubit connectivity, quantum unmonored learning maintains high accuracy. Additionally, we observed that the instruct IQL algorithm can enhance recognition performance, yielding either equal or superior results to the unmonored approach.

We propose an enhancement to the FastPitch system that significantly expands its pitch controllability. While the original iteration could only approximate pitches by relying on captured speaker capabilities and lacked specific techniques for creating unnatural pitches, our method employs pitch augmentation. This is achieved by applying cycle-consistent gan (CCGAN) based on timbre preservation to stabilize the synthesis output. To utilize this augmented signal in synthesis, we suggest a new approach for estimating timbre preservation that addresses limitations in existing metrics. Combined, these strategies double the set of synthesize-able pitch ranges while maintaining or improving speech naturalness.

The architecture relies on a multi-modal encoder paired with an innovative graph-based representation strategy. This system facilitates deep spatiotemporal analysis by enabling the model to perform multiple reasoning steps by retrieving and processing relevant information across different temporal instances. Additionally, "Hopper" demonstrates robust performance on the AMTQA benchmark—a dataset featuring diverse temporal contexts, objects, state variations, and question types—achieving a top-tier result of 68.1% accuracy.

This study utilizes 2D hydrodynamic simulations to model the final stage of gas protoplanetary disk evolution involving two massive Jupiter-like bodies growing to approximately 3 Jupiter masses ($\sim$3 MJ) over a period of $\sim$100,000 years. The primary objectives are to quantify the impact of a depleted reservoir on the total accretion rate, planet mass, and the morphological state of the disk, with specific focus on gas kinematics and dust vertical structure. The analysis reveals three key findings: (i) in a massive Jupiter scenario, gas accretion is controlled by the shrinking of the corotation shock radius rather than by disk viscosity, (ii) depletion of gas supply results in significantly lower accretion rates, yielding two planets of $\sim$2.5 MJ and one disk edge planet of $\sim$3 MJ, while gas abundance maintains planets of $\sim$3 MJ; (iii) dust settling is accelerated by turbulence damping, causing vertical dust distribution to shift from a Gaussian profile to a sharp interface, and while dust trapping in pressure maxima is common, dust migration is significantly slower than the growth timescale of planets. The study concludes that dust accumulation at pressure maxima is insufficient to significantly impact planet growth, and gas kinematics are significantly altered by mutual drag forces, with the outer disk edge being significantly depleted and modified.

Electrons within a bundle of carbon nanotubes are assumed to be isolated to individual tubes, a premise contradicted by this study. Using terahertz time-domain spectroscopy, we experimentally demonstrate that electrical transport across an insulating polymer shell surrounding the nanotubes occurs. This coupled electron-intube system exchanges charge with phononic modes of the supporting scaffold at a temperature-dependent rate. These findings enhance our comprehension of electronics in nanoscale composite materials and offer potential pathways for engineering electronic properties through phonon-mediated mechanisms.

Introducing a novel clustering algorithm termed Entropy-driven Variable Feature Weighted fuzzy k-means (EVFW), a method designed to address the shifting relevance of features in fuzzy contexts. Unlike the conventional Fuzzy clustering algorithm (FWK), EVFW assigns dynamic importance metrics to the original features. The framework utilizes entropy values to measure each feature's divergence from the average dataset distribution, thereby generating corresponding feature weights. Furthermore, an analytical proof demonstrates that EVFW converges to a stable cluster configuration and reaches an objective function minimum. The algorithm is evaluated across both synthetic datasets and real-world data, specifically from the UCI repository. Comparative evaluations against established fuzzy clustering algorithms in (1) high-dimensional settings, (2) scenarios with varying intrinsic feature counts, and (3) cases where underlying data distributions exhibit disparate densities, demonstrate superior performance by EVFW.

Mixture-of-Expert (MSE) is an optimization problem that has been a popular approach for training neural networks since the 1980s. Despite its widespread adoption in various domains, the primary drawback remains the tendency for over-fitting. This issue arises because the objective function is non-convex, causing the optimization process to become trapped in local minima where experts specialize excessively and subsequently enter deadlocks. To address challenges posed by MSE's non-convexity, this research introduces two novel algorithms: Variational Mix-Expert (VME) and Expert-Jensen-Shannon-Join (EJS-JS). By leveraging variational inference and Bayesian principles, these methods mitigate expert specialization, resulting in smoother posterior distributions. Furthermore, a key advantage of VME and its related algorithms is their ability to seamlessly integrate into existing frameworks, such as the Deadlines in MSE (DME). This paper also presents two distinct algorithms for handling expert-JS-JS: a batch-based approach and another that operates efficiently without requiring access to the entire dataset at once. These methods offer a robust solution for managing large-scale datasets efficiently. Finally, the paper provides an implementation of both VME and its related algorithms in the form of a library that supports multi-GPUs for efficient computation. This study examines the constraints on global symmetry within quantum gravity models derived from analyzing cosmic birefringence, focusing specifically on recent 2-point function data from Planck's B-mode polarization maps. Specifically, it investigates the phase rotation affecting linearly polarized light from distant gravitational sources. The analysis utilizes both the CMB's 2-point function and reconstructed galaxy cluster lensing of the background CMB polarization. Global symmetries are theorized to undergo spontaneous breaking at high energy scales, potentially leading to small violations of the phase of linear polarization for linearly polarized light from distant gravitational sources. The study finds that the universal phase shift of linear polarization is restricted by Planck lensing of the background GRB to be less than 0.03 radians at a 95% confidence level. This finding rules out quantum gravity frameworks where effective fields remain unbroken below $10^ {17}$ eV and suggests that effective fields remain unbroken below $^{17}$ eV.

We utilized UVIT data from the Aditya-L1 mission to analyze the UV luminous star (ULLS) population within the globular cluster NGC 4147. Following the application of UV luminosity function techniques, we identified 11 candidate blue stars. To validate their status as true ULLS and rule out contamination from blue horizontal branch (BHB) or blue giant (BG) stars, we conducted proper motion studies using V-band imagery from the Hubble Space Telescope. The analysis revealed that the ULLS in NGC 4147 share the same proper motion as the red giant branch (RGB) and red giant branch horizontal (RGBH) stars. This observation confirms that ULLS are genuine members of this ancient globular cluster rather than field stars. Additionally, we observed a correlation between the UBLs' UV magnitudes and their V-band brightness, suggesting they are not blue giant (BG) objects. The spatial distribution of these UBLs appears random, lacking any relation to the cluster core. The ages of UBLs in NGC 4147 could be explained by either binary systems or horizontal branch (HB) variations. However, the high helium fraction (Y) and low temperature of UBLs in NGC 4147 strongly suggest that binary systems are unlikely contributors to the observed population.

Transfer learning is widely employed to enhance the performance of deep learning models across various domains. In this research, we revisit two fundamental transferability guarantees and their underlying reasons. Our findings demonstrate that these rules are limited to specific scenarios and do not universally hold. By integrating the concepts of representation representation and domain alignment, we introduce a comprehensive new criterion for assessing the transferability of labels. Leveraging this criterion, we developed a new method to learn domain-adapted representations that are 20% to 40% more effective at predicting source domain labels on the target domain compared to existing methods, according to our experiments.

Effective communication is vital for social dynamics, economic interactions, and contagious processes like disease or rumor spread. While the impact of social networks on these phenomena has been extensively studied, the underlying mechanisms governing information dissemination remain incompletely understood. We contend that network modularity—a measure of intra-group homogeneity and inter-group heterogeneity—is a critical determinant in regulating the velocity of information spread. Our findings indicate a non-linear relationship: as modular increases, the speed of dissemination accelerates initially but eventually slows down as modular reaches high levels. Importantly, the relationship holds across diverse structural configurations, whether networks feature a single module or multiple distinct clusters of varying sizes. We demonstrate that these insights apply to both homogeneous size partitions and heterogeneous size partitions. Our research further reveals the relationship is robust across varying degrees of internal and external connection strengths within and between communities. Beyond theoretical understanding, these results hold true for real-world datasets from multiple social contexts.

The Thomas-Yau distinctiveness framework serves as a framework for defining entropy on surfaces within Riemannian 3-manifolds as the entropy of volume-normalized minimal surfaces holding constant mean curvature. Building on this foundation, this paper introduces the concept of *distinctiveness with quantitative parameters* and explores its properties through the framework of entropy. The study demonstrates that within a ball in $\mathbb{R}^3$, Chua and Knorz's distinctiveness theorem aligns with the new concept, and reveals a relationship between distinctiveness and expansion through the framework of entropy.

The time-domain standard perturbation model offers computational efficiency by utilizing the linearization of a nonlinear system around a fixed-point operating within a simulation. Although widely adopted for system-level evaluation of unamplified links, its impact on perturbation-induced errors remains unparsed. This study introduces a timing perturbation model tailored for such links and defines the critical threshold of reference-time error tolerance. Given the difficulty in quantifying this limit a priori, a convergence acceleration algorithm is proposed to expediate determination. This methodology calculates the error metric across a discrete spectrum of perturbed reference times, culminating in the identification of the point at which criteria for tolerance are met and the boundary is established.

This study examines research into Android's issue-space evasion attacks, a technique where malicious apps exploit isolated components like the Intent service or File Manager to bypass security restrictions. The work categorizes and analyzes the Android literature in this domain, focusing on specific issues, underlying mechanisms, and countermeasures.

The survey analyzes 15 published evasion attacks targeting individual OS issues. These cases demonstrate how adversaries manipulate system behaviors to circumvent protections, with implications for both understanding vulnerabilities and developing future defenses.

The analysis further examines attacks targeting four specific operating system issues—namely Intent, File, Input, and Input Method Manager—detailing their operational mechanisms.

Finally, the paper reviews issue-evading countermeasures that rely on system-level modifications. These approaches aggregate behavioral data to detect anomalies and refine system designs to enhance robustness, thereby strengthening the OS against such threats.

This paper introduces Ozy, a universal orchestration platform designed to handle tasks across diverse execution environments, including cloud services, edge networks, and on-premises systems, while also supporting air-gapped networks. By abstracting execution environments, it enables the deployment of high-availability applications without the need for environment-specific adjustments. Unlike current approaches, the proposal presents a new method for managing task dependencies that relies on optimizing resource utilization rather than depending on precise prediction models. This enhancement leads to significant improvements in efficiency, performance, and cost, while boosting reliability and reducing latency. The authors validate these advantages through a comprehensive evaluation of various network topologies and deployment scenarios.

The quantum Hall (QH) ferrotic phase, which emerges from coupling Landau levels within an effective Heisenberg model featuring both symmetric and antisymmetric exchange interactions, is examined. We reveal a reentrant behavior of this phase at moderate strengths of the redshift parameter (Landau-level-coupling), a phenomenon attributed to the $\sigma_z$-type exchange interaction. Through a combination of variational and numerical approaches, along with an analysis of the effective Hamiltonian, we demonstrate that the fundamental quantum Hall ground state interacts with low-lying excitations, resulting in the exchange of the antisymmetric interaction driving the phase to reappear. Furthermore, the system exhibits another form known as the $\sigma_\mu$ exchange force.

The authors argue that both positions are flawed and that prior constraints placed on primordial black holes (PBHs) regarding their potential contribution to dark matter—derived from LIGO-Virgo observations of binary mergers—remain valid for CBHs. This study investigates the planetesimal density variance generated during planet formation via pebble accretion, specifically targeting the formation of a super-Earth core within a minimum mass disk scenario. Utilizing a radial model that accounts for the random walk of pressure-drift flusctuations and variations in core growth rates, we examine multiple scenarios. Results indicate a substantial spread in planetesimal densities, varying by nearly an order of magnitude, with the core forming at a mean specific energy of $3.2 \pm 1.2 \text{ Gg/cc}$. Crucially, we demonstrate that local density fluctuations are primarily driven by variations in core growth rates rather than direct density fluctuations. Furthermore, unlike density variations, the planetesimal mass distribution exhibits minimal spread. Importantly, varying density assumptions significantly impact the planet formation timescale, potentially accounting for discrepancies between standard models and the actual formation duration of Earth and Venus.

Overparameterized models have achieved remarkable success in numerous machine learning domains, a phenomenon this study explains by investigating the link between model generalization and computational constraints. We demonstrate that within a generalized linear model (GLR) framework, an exponentially large number of parameters can be an advantage provided that exact global optima are unattainable within suboptimal local optima exist, ensuring good generalization. Conversely, if the data dimension is low enough that computational feasibility allows finding global solutions, a smaller parameter space becomes essential. We substantiate these theoretical findings empirically using both synthetic benchmarks and real-world datasets. Additionally, we verify that these principles extend beyond linear models, observing the same behavior in deep neural networks where massive capacities paradoxically facilitate superior generalization. Despite their overparameterization, well-performing models for GLM tasks exhibit strong sparsity patterns: when analyzed under a restricted singular value decomposition (RSVD), only approximately a polynomial fraction of components are necessary to represent the information content, with the remaining parameters having negligible impact.

This paper presents and investigates an algorithmic solution to an operational problem faced by \textit{M\'etropolitain Dial-a-Ride} (MDAR), a specialized transport service connecting individuals with mobility challenges in Paris. The original objective involves generating a fleet of routes to satisfy all travel requests within the MDAR system. However, real-world operational constraints require that routes not only fulfill all travel demands but also adhere to strict capacity limits, vehicle speed, and parking availability at various locations. Because these additional constraints are often overlooked by standard routing algorithms used for pure dial-a-ride problems, traditional approaches must be modified to incorporate them. To address these practical limitations, we have developed a novel algorithm incorporating capacity limits, vehicle speed, and parking availability into its design. This new algorithm is based on branch-and-cut techniques, integrating constraint programming into the model to enhance its performance. Our computational experiments demonstrate that the algorithm effectively generates an optimal fleet of routes satisfying all travel requests while also adhering to vehicle capacity limits, vehicle speed, and parking availability constraints.

This paper introduces K9, our proposed multi-modal pre-training framework designed to recognize knowledge across both images and text within the e-commerce domain. We have developed K9Express, a specialized model built upon the K9 pre-training model that integrates explicit entity and relationship alignment signals derived from a Knowledge Graph to enhance performance in downstream tasks. Evaluations on a E-commerce Knowledge Graph containing over 10k entities and 15k relationships demonstrate the effectiveness of K9Pre for zero-shot entity prediction across diverse vantage points and regions, as well as for multi-view sentiment analysis. Additionally, K9Express successfully surpasses baseline models in its ability to support the knowledge graph completion and recommendation tasks prevalent in electronic commerce.

The escalating incidence of Alzheimer's ailment (AA) imposes a severe socioeconomic burden on modern society. While risk factors such as age, sex, and family history are established, the precise etiology remains elusive. The early detection of non-modifiable risk factors offers a viable pathway for prevention or mitigation of this condition. This study introduces the novel application of the Deep InfoMax (DIM) framework—a framework designed to extract causal risk cues from observed variables—to a comprehensive cohort dataset. This dataset encompasses detailed clinical history, risk factors, and Alzheimer's progression status. Our analysis indicates that the genetic inheritance (family history) and the presence of the ApoE4 allele are the sole risk factors exhibiting causal relationships with AA advancement. These findings align with existing medical literature. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first empirical demonstration supporting family history as a causal factor for AA progression. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the genetic composition (specificity of haplotypes within the ApoE gene) constitutes another causal indicator of disease progression.

While recent studies have explored various methods for inferring language models, few address step-by-step execution. This paper proposes a novel, iterative dynamic model designed to generate interpretations for higher-order functions, reciting results of lambda-term computation involving lambda-terms. Our model relies on an iteration-driven, recurrent network structure, learning from the discrepancy between predicted and ground truth answers. The model demonstrates the ability to learn syntax-specific mechanisms, such as abstractions, and effectively execute execution plans derived from language specifications. The results highlight that an iteration-recurrent network is well-suited for learning the complexities of programming language semantics.

Spin-orbit coupling in transition metal oxides is typically weak, but we demonstrate that strong magnetic fluctuations enhance this interaction significantly. Using *ab initio* many-body perturbation theory grounded in density functional theory, we calculated the spin-dependent electron self-energy for the strongly correlated metal La2NiIrO6. Our findings indicate that magnetic fluctuations amplifying near a quantum critical point significantly boost the bulk effective spin-orbit interaction. Specifically, in bulk La2NiIrO6, this internally generated contribution is roughly double the total effective value, aligning with recent experimental findings. However, in a hypothetical hypothetical ferromagnetic state where such fluctuations are removed, the perturbation theory predicts a self-energy contribution that is 100% smaller than the total effect. These results underscore the necessity of accounting for strong fluctuations when determining effective spin-orbit interactions in correlated systems.

We demonstrate that liquids adhering to a power-law adiabatic law ($P \propto \rho^\Gamma$) with $\Gamma > 1$ possess a conformal shadow. This optical medium supports a conformal symmetry and propagates light at a velocity precisely equal to that of sound. Notably, this shadow substance exhibits confinement and fermionic statistics. Within this framework, the fundamental particles (shadow matter) emerge as the only robust low-energy degrees of freedom of the underlying fluid, generalizing the behavior of QCD in the high-temperature, high-density regime where quarks serve as simple low-energy modes of a complex liquid.

Regulatory bodies are increasingly recognizing the challenges associated with deploying and monitoring medical device software in clinical practice distribution shifts pose significant risks by rendering these systems ineffective or unsafe when deployed on data sources that differ from training distributions. To address this, we introduce a framework for monitoring and evaluating the statistical performance of black-box AI medical diagnostic tools. Our proposed approach employs two methods to assess an estimator's confidence under distribution shifts: the first calculates the expected error rate of the optimal classifier using U-statistics, while the second generates prediction intervals for the class being estimated. We demonstrate that the classification error estimates remain stable across various distribution shifts and show stronger out-of-sample efficacy compared to the empirical distribution, particularly with limited data. Additionally, the forecast-based confidence indicator successfully identifies distribution shifts earlier than the optimal true positive rate. These findings suggest our framework offers valuable insights for assessing the statistical performance of black-box AI diagnostic tools under distribution shifts, especially regarding regulatory compliance.

We introduce the Stiff Base Biasing (SBB) approach to facilitate enhanced sampling of DNA conformations within all-atom simulations. This method builds upon the well-established concept of uniform sampling via canonical (NVT) ensembles by restricting local conformational variations to specific bases while locking the remainder in their current states via optimized constraints optimized to minimize perturbation to natural DNA dynamics. By broadening the landscape of accessible localized conformational states, sampling occurs more efficiently. Initial tests on a B-DNA system reveal that, contrary to the limitations of standard B3C3 conformation analysis methods, sampling remains adequate. Furthermore, root mean square fluctuation (RMSF) profiles exhibit a high correlation with standard dynamics results, and base-pair step mechanics remain largely consistent with typical B-DNA behavior. Given its simplicity, SBB is applicable not only to DNA but also to other macromolecular systems, extending beyond the typical scope of molecular dynamics methods focused solely on macromolecular interactions.

The development of dielectric techniques to identify and characterize pore fluid in cement-based materials has been significantly advanced by the work of various research teams. The initial challenge involved creating a porous medium model to guide the subsequent design of an experimental protocol for extracting cement paste dielectric spectra. The resulting experimental workflow enabled the characterization of key materials parameters, including the bulk dielectric permittivity, electrical conductivity, and relaxation times. The primary objective was to determine if pore fluid properties could be isolated from those of the solid matrix. While the study achieved this goal, it is acknowledged that the measured relaxation times represent a composite of relaxation mechanisms occurring in both phases. Furthermore, the inability to uniquely separate conductivity values for the fluid and solid phases remains a limitation. Despite these hurdles, the established methodology offers a robust framework for analyzing cementitious materials and other porous media.

This work introduces a new clustering algorithm, "Heavy-heavy," designed to prioritize the identification of heavy hadronic clusters. Utilizing "pseudoprofiles," a novel concept introduced here, the algorithm can operate in both event-by-event and evt-averaged modes. By combining the event-wise "Heavy-heavy" approach with the Fast Brachistochrone (FBI) technique, a new hybrid called "Heavy-FBI" has been developed; this method not only maintains the original detection capabilities but also significantly boosts processing speed. These algorithms were tested using data from proton-lead (p+Pb) collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV recorded by ALICE in energy density regimes comparable to those in heavy-ion collisions studied in prior research, with an additional analysis of proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV. Both simulations and experimental results indicate a strong production of pionic clusters, whereas the yields for clusters composed of nucleons and heavy flavor particles are significantly lower.

This research introduces a novel approach to analyzing the progressive development of military swarms of drones through natural language processing. By employing Natural Language Understanding (NLU), the method seeks to extract specific textual features and metadata from NLU sources, converting this unstructured data into a numerical format. Consequently, it enables machine learning algorithms to process the information, allowing for the prediction of advancements in military drone swarms. This study also evaluates various algorithms and data sources—specifically Wikipedia, JSTOR, and WST (JSTOR USA)—utilizing metadata from patent documents. The metadata was processed via the SOTA transformer model BERT and converted into vectors. Finally, the vector data was input into five distinct machine learning algorithms for analysis and forecasting.

Predicting human trajectory is a time-critical domain that requires understanding social interactions. However, current approaches often rely on computationally expensive, non-real-time, global search methods. To address this, we introduce a socially-aware, sliding-window-based, sequential latent latent-space embedding framework. This approach leverages a cognitive model of goal-directed navigation, enhanced by an innovative Social Cognition View (SCV) module that enables efficient, localized trajectory forecasting. Specifically, the SCV module allows agents to perceive neighboring movement patterns within a constrained latent framework and anticipate future paths within a sliding prediction horizon. Experimental results on the well-known GTZA and ETH/UCSD datasets confirm that this prediction framework is both computationally efficient and precise, while maintaining limited memory requirements.

This study investigates the measures of mutual information between the network's input and output layers to evaluate the inherent complexity introduced by different architectures. Our results indicate that in a Boltzmann machine, increasing the mask size used to connect input and output layers significantly elevates the complexity, even when the hidden layer's dimensions remain unchanged. Conversely, the impact of varying the number of neurons in the intermediate layer is minimal. These findings allow for the optimization of existing architectures or the design of new ones by leveraging these metrics for the efficient modeling of complex distributions. Moreover, the analysis reveals that deterministic autoencoders exhibit greater overall complexity than their probabilistic counterparts, a distinction that persists across diverse network structures.

Recognized as a natural interface, sequential hand gesture detection facilitates human-swarm collaboration through a chain of movements. Previous research primarily utilized this capability for individual-computer engagement, employing deep learning to map hand motions into categories. In contrast, this study introduces a new framework designed specifically for distributed interactions across distributed systems, focusing on dynamic tag assignment among various predefined hand gestures executed sequentially. Our proposed solution leverages an LSTM-driven deep learning framework capable of generating probabilistic outputs, allowing for real-time identification of gestures performed in the physical space alongside the associated confidence levels.

We investigate the impact of the stellar wind on accretion in black hole systems by analyzing the X-ray data from the high-mass binary Cyg X-1. Using simultaneous observations from NuSTAR and MAXI, we examined spectral and temporal data to determine the properties of a potential "stellar breeze." The spectral analysis reveals a hard power-law component with a photon index of $\Gamma = 1.67 \pm 0.02$, overlaid with minor Fe K$\alpha$ emission. This model fits the observed light curves better, revealing that the count rate variability in the soft band is significantly amplified, while the hard band variability remains largely unchanged. Furthermore, we extracted higher-fidelity cross-correlation lags between bands; the results confirm a pattern of phase lag hardening, where soft radiation trails hard radiation. These findings are consistent with a two-zone radiative model of optically thin accretion disc annuli. The data also indicate that a component of the Cyg X-1 accretion originates from the stellar wind.

The edge states of both the three-dimensional (3D) and two-dimensional (2D) topological insulators (TIs) are defined by a non-Abelian effective field theory. This work examines a non-Abelian ether-like term within that theory, which lacks Lorentz invariance yet remains Weyl-invariant and generally well-defined in $d+1$ dimensions without relying on a specific metric. To determine the ether-like term's coefficient, we employ the Feynman-Schwinger parametrization combined with a proper-time integral to compute the one-loop self-energy of Dirac fermions in Lorentz-invariant backgrounds, thereby generalizing the calculation of thermal one-loop fermion self-energy to $d+1$ dimensions. We utilize the ether-like term in the stochastic heat equation to investigate thermal boundary heat transport, specifically analyzing the influence of spatial and temporal non-localities on heat diffusivity derived from the self-energy. Finally, we construct a non-Abelian analog of the Anderson-Hubbard model to explore the thermal Hall effect within these states, generalizing the input ether-like term from the bulk to their boundaries.

Although universal semantic models utilizing embeddings have gained prominence, the specific field of language modeling remains grounded in syntactic techniques. This work introduces an approach that leverages theory-informed, syntactic-collaborative universal models to enhance model performance through a dual-level strategy. Initially, we develop a UPOS-Embedding for universal part-of-speech tags, learning vector representations that capture the relationships among individual tags. Subsequently, we integrate these location-aware positional encodings, derived from syntactic tags, into a word-embedding matrix. This allows for a more precise localization of input sequences. Experimental results demonstrate that this methodology yields significant performance improvements across all languages. This advancement underscores the continued utility of syntactic models and suggests that the integration of external linguistic knowledge can substantially boost universal language modeling capabilities.

We examine the impact of magnetized ejecta on the post-merger dynamics of neutrino-cool accretion disks following the collapse of massive binaries. Drawing on a series of 2D hydrodynamic simulations, this study investigates how such ejecta alters the evolution of remnant disks, specifically in the context of heavy element production and the formation of fast outflows. By executing a 1D radiation-transfer calculation, we assess how these perturbations to the disk's composition and dynamics influence the synthesis of r-process elements. Our results indicate that an outflow with a mass of $0.01\,M_{\odot}$ can shift the abundance pattern of the resulting r-process elements if the ejecta originates from the disk. However, we find that an outflow with a higher mass of $0.1\,M_{\odot}$—if it instead arises from the ejecta phase of the binary merger itself—can effectively obscure the chemical signature originally imprinted by the disk.

Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are brief, millisecond-duration cosmic radio signals that remain a subject of debate regarding their origin. This review paper provides a comprehensive overview of advancements in modeling and control, focusing on the Model-Based Control (MBC) approach. We examine various models used to represent the kinematics and dynamics required for soft robot manipulation. Furthermore, the study critically analyzes two primary MBC control methods—Internal Model-Based (IMB) and External Model-Based (EMB)—along with the associated optimization and control theory. The paper also highlights the critical role of constitutive material models and finite element analysis (FEA) tools in the soft robotics landscape. Finally, we outline the current limitations within the field and propose a roadmap for future research aimed at overcoming these obstacles.

We reestablish the realization of the Jacobi group as a real Lie group. By reexamining its action on the Siegel upper-half space, this study establishes the convergence of the associated Lie algebra representation derived from distribution functions on the group. Furthermore, this work relates this Lie algebra representation explicitly to the Maass representation on the Siegel space and finally relates these structures to the authentic Jacobi group through a Lie algebra isomorphism.

We challenge the assumption that table summarization techniques transfer effectively to large tables, specifically regarding the confirmation of facts derived solely from a standard subset of the table. While previous approaches to table summarization have primarily focused on table-wide interpretation, we demonstrate that many errors stem from this broad perspective. We propose an alternative strategy that breaks tables into smaller components to enhance summarization accuracy and that limits inference strictly to the provided table excerpt. We also provide open-sourced annotations for over 1,000 tables from the T-REx dataset to support future research. Experiments on this new, extensive dataset reveal that standard large language models frequently commit table-wide hallucinations and that many valid facts in T-REx are actually invalid when evaluated against a complete table. To improve factorization of T-REx and increase valid factorization, we introduce Table2Table which uses a two-stage pipeline to extract information incrementally from a source table to a target table. We further demonstrate that this method can improve the accuracy of LLMs in confirming facts and locate specific failures in their reasoning. We also show that prompt engineering, including prompt tuning and prompt pruning, are effective in reducing the hallucination of LLMs when they are used to extract information from a source table to a target table. Conditioned Generative Adversarial Networks (CondGANs) are a technique for producing images from target distributions based on an input class label. This research investigates a novel approach where the generator's latent space is partially determined by conditioning signals within a novel framework termed Hidden Space Conditioning (HSC). Unlike traditional methods that assign conditions directly to the generator, HSC first transforms conditions into another set of latent variables and subsequently samples from a conditioned distribution to establish the final generator latent state. Despite the increased complexity of learning signal representations compared to direct mapping, this simple shift in mechanism demonstrates superior performance across multiple tasks. This structure also opens new research avenues, specifically by enhancing both label privacy and multi-label support.

Traditional Gibbs samplers for discrete distributions are often criticized for generating highly correlated sequences that yield slow convergence when the target distribution becomes increasingly concentrated on a smaller subset of its support. Contrastingly, the concept of "partial reversibility," exemplified by the heat-bath sampler using local full reversibility, has been the focus of extensive study, particularly within graph theory and statistical physics. However, a generalized version—the "step sampler"—has received far less attention despite its potential to be substantially more rapid under specific conditions.

Our primary objective involves establishing the superiority of step samplers over Gibbs types specifically layered distributions, a subclass where target distributions concentrate progressively within layered structures. Our findings indicate two distinct scenarios where step samplers possess strictly superior worst-case asymptotic convergence rates compared to Gibbs samplers. Furthermore, our structural analysis demonstrates that even outside these optimal cases, step samplers maintain advantageous properties by exhibiting a higher spectral gap and fewer reversed steps in the contrast with standard Gibbs mechanisms.

Recent deep learning approaches for out-of-distribution detection typically train a mapping network to transform input data into a vector field representing a probability distribution, such as a Gaussian. These methods assess the location of query points relative to this distribution to determine their distribution status. However, such vectors often fail to capture the full shape of the true data distribution. To address this, we introduce a new architecture featuring multiple normal distribution layers for better representation and analysis. Our study reveals that standard neural network layers for vector field regression are prone to catastrophic overfitting, causing them to collapse into a single distribution vector field rather than maintaining local structure. We mitigate this issue using a new regularizer based on distributional normal processes (DNPs), which fosters more robust and accurate vector field learning. We further demonstrate that DNP layers can effectively capture the underlying structure of data distributions. Empirical evaluations confirm the method's superior performance in learning this structure and remain state-of-the-art in identifying out-of-distributions across three benchmark datasets.

This study examines a one-dimensional lattice system subjected to periodic driving and optical pumping. The researchers discovered that the adiabatically modified eigenstates of such an inherently discrete systems can be altered to mimic continuous space via Floquet engineering and specific discrete lattice patterns. They outline two distinct approaches to achieve this transformation: first, by optimizing the adiabatically shifted eigenstates using a scar-like configuration within the lattice, and second, by shaping the adiabatically shifted states into near-continuous distributions through careful lattice pattern design.

Furthermore, the authors investigate under what conditions the system can achieve Fermi-Dirac-like or Bose-Einstein-Condensation (BEC)-like distributions. While thermal equilibrium distributions are typically expected in open and non-equilibrium systems, the study demonstrates that the lattice geometry combined with drive amplitude can generate these non-equilibrium distributions. Specifically, they find that increasing driver strength leads to a transition from Fermi-Dirac-like to Bose- like behavior, and that carefully tuning the lattice parameters can induce a "quasi-BEC" in the system.

Ultimately, the work provides theoretical support for engineering novel many-body quantum phenomena in open, pumped-dissipative systems by leveraging non-trivial adiabatic eigenstates combined with precise lattice architectures.

This study addresses the dynamic real-time provisioning of Service Function Chains (SFCs) within fog-assisted Software-Defined Networking (SDN) environments that are subjected to link and switch failures. The VNF instances hosted on network edge servers benefit from the proximity to end-users, offering low-latency applications and enhanced Quality of Service (QoS). To ensure robust operation and maintain these quality standards, multiple VNFs are deployed across several servers to facilitate rapid failover in failure scenarios. The paper introduces an energy-efficient resource management system that leverages dynamic server management techniques to reduce both energy consumption and VNF processing latency. The primary goal is to real-time SFC provisioning that minimizes latency and energy usage and energy costs. The research focuses on two key challenges: (1) developing a joint failure restoration and energy-efficient resource management strategy to ensure rapid SFC recovery and reduced server costs, and (2) implementing a fault mitigation technique to prevent specific links or switches from causing further issues. The proposed solution is formulated as a Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model and is evaluated using the EventSimulator, a new network simulator designed to assess the performance of the suggested approach.

Loss functions are pivotal components in machine learning that directly influence model training and performance. However, designing an effective loss function remains challenging, as existing designs often result from intuition or trial-and-error. This paper employs gradient surgery to theoretically analyze and interpret common loss functions, enabling a clearer understanding of their specific influences on trained models. Through these insights, we offer an enhanced comprehension of the function $\\text{loss}(y, pred) = \\text{ce}(y, pred)^\\gamma$ used in $\\gamma$-cross-entropy for classification. This theoretical analysis complements our experimental findings, which demonstrate that this parameterized form performs as well as or better than standard cross-entropy across multiple datasets for tasks like image and video classification.

We propose a new class of holographic codes termed Hyper-Invariant MERA (HIMERA), characterized by scale-invariant, scale-free correlation functions that strictly limit the length of stabilizer generators. Within a discrete setting, this system maps to a hyperbolic lattice where the code is supported on the entire lattice points. In the continuum limit, the associated stabilizers generate a hyper-singular operator with non-local support, and the error correction process is governed by a non-local action derived from the measure of hyperbolic volume. This framework yields an approximate, yet near-optimal encoding of error correction, with the code capacity approaching full support within a factor of two.

This paper addresses the difficulty of maintaining stable voltage levels across modern distribution networks, which are constantly exposed to high voltage surges caused by unpredictable load fluctuations and the addition of new generation sources. To solve this, we develop a distributed two-tier voltage regulation approach. The primary layer utilizes centralized algorithms, such as Distributed Gradient Projection (DGP), to determine optimal transformer tap settings. In parallel, the secondary layer employs distributed methods—specifically the Distributed Average Consensus (DAC) protocol—to propagate appropriate target voltages to each node. The effectiveness of these strategies is validated through simulations on a 123-bus test system.

This paper examines a model featuring multiple specialized agents, each capable of executing only one of two available tasks. For each task, the cumulative earnings are stochastic but have a positive drift, with the mean reward rate's uncertainty diminishing with repeated trials. Agents select tasks based on current estimates of instantaneous rewards, and the process continues until one agent's total earnings strictly exceed the other by a specified threshold.

Because each agent exhibits task specialization, the expected completion time will surpass that of single-task agents, a finding we confirm persists even when agents exhibit no such specialization. In the scenario involving general non-specialized agents, the completion time grows at most as the square root ($\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$) of threshold $n$, assuming optimal strategies. However, for specialists, the completion time scales linearly with $n$ ($\Theta(n)$), provided agents act using greedy policies. We also establish that the linear-growth bound for specialists, when agents are perfectly rational, holds regardless of the specific reward distributions or parameters.

We further demonstrate that the linear-time asymptotic limit ($\Theta(n)$) is not exclusive to specific agent behaviors or task structures, but can be observed in broader classes of tasks and for task-dependent processing delays.
