Dialogue is a fundamental human capability, and recent years have seen significant advancements in text-generation technology. However, many current models still rely on human annotations for training, which are expensive and time-consuming. We introduce a structured training method that enables machines to acquire natural, human-like conversational abilities directly from raw text without requiring manual labeling. Specifically, we leverage the turn-taking architecture of dialogue to train the model on the next speaker prediction task. This data-driven method produces conversational outputs that are experimentally shown to be more human-like than those generated by standard baseline approaches.

studies of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) under finite net baryon density exhibit significantly greater complexity compared to the well-understood QCD phase diagram at zero net baryon density. These studies are driven by the necessity to interpret a wide array of experimental data, including heavy-ion collision results, lattice QCD calculations, and diverse nuclear physics experiments involving atomic nuclei. A defining characteristic of the QCD phase diagram under dense conditions is the presence of the so-called "triangle point," representing a location where two or three distinct phases coexist. This section provides an overview of the current experimental and theoretical landscape, with a particular emphasis on recent lattice QCD advancements.

We introduce a statistical approach for predicting offshore wind turbine loads as a function of environmental and operational variables. By embedding Gaussian processes into a sequential model structured to match the time hierarchy of load components, the method accounts for the multi-scale nature of these signals. The proposed technique constructs surrogate models that replace complex, high-fidelity simulations or field data for use in load or power forecasting and the analysis of load extremes and distributions. Utilating loads from the OpenFAST simulator across a range of the SC70 turbine environmental scenarios, the study evaluates the model's performance using standard error metrics for prediction accuracy. It further analyzes the surrogate data to predict Extreme Energy Levels and specific load distributions, demonstrating that the Gaussian process framework offers a flexible tool for integrating diverse environmental inputs and environmental regimes.

This paper presents an examination of Twitter activity in its aftermath, utilizing the 2020 Izmir earthquake in Turkey as a case study. By analyzing the tweets, we aimed to evaluate the platform's potential for disaster response management. Specifically, we investigated Twitter's official policies regarding disaster management and compared the official responses of the @IZMIRATSMV account against user-generated content. Utilizing the VADER (Very weak Dependency-based Sentiment ScOrer) to gauge sentiment, we found that user-generated crisis responses significantly outnumber those of the official account, albeit with the latter posting more frequently. User tweets were also found to be more positive than official ones. Despite the disparity in response sentiment, the overall mixture indicates a slight negative tilt. Ultimately, the study concludes that gridders should not only focus on negative user feedback but also leverage the high proportion of user-positive tweets to enhance disaster management strategies.

A group $G$ is defined as $R_\infty$ if each of its homomorphisms into groups possessing exactly two distinct elements yields an $R_\infty$-group; this behavior has been identified for various classes, ranging from metabelian and $(N-2)$-step nilpotent groups to $F$-nilpotent groups. The present research investigates whether generalized solvable Baumslag-Solier groups, $B_\mathrm{gen}(m,n)$—extensions of the standard solvable $BS\langle m,n\rangle\ltent\mathbb{Z}\rigr)$ that remain not $\ltent n=1\rtend\rigr)-$cyclic under the Hirsch length—exhibit the $R_\infty$-property by focusing on their free nilpotent quotients of step length. The findings indicate that while the property fails when $|\lvert n\rvert =1$, it holds true whenever $\gcd\langle m,n\rangle =1$ and $\lvert n\rvert\gtend 1$. Furthermore, we establish that every nilpotent quotient of step length satisfying $\lvert N-2\rvert \lend 1$ for the generalized group is an $R_\infty$-group.

This research introduces a novel framework for inverse optimization of time-varying data within a trajectory approach. By integrating a ODE solver with a steepest descent algorithm, the method iteratively refines both model parameters and initial states to minimize a cost function, which quantifies the discrepancy between simulated trajectories and empirical observations. The efficiency of this iterative process is significantly enhanced through the application of an adjoint-sensitivity tangent-stickiness framework. Extensive tests using synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that the algorithm can accurately recover dynamic states and parameters from noisy or incomplete partial data. Notably, the algorithm is capable of identifying multiple distinct local optima, thereby enabling the detection of alternative trajectories inherent in the system. Empirical evaluations confirm that the proposed method effectively maps nonlinear transformations, revealing the algorithm's potential to resolve the latent internal states of complex systems.

Naturalistic Driving Datasets (NDDs) are essential for advancing research in driver behavior, safety, human factors, and automated driving. Yet, laboratory settings often fail to provide sufficient contextural richness for developing effective driver assistance systems. In response, researchers have created datasets capturing real-world driving. Despite this progress, these datasets often lack detailed situational context required to interpret driving decisions effectively. To address this gap, we introduce the Situation-based Naturalistic Driving Dataset (SceNDD), a massive repository comprising real-world driving trajectories paired with comprehensive situational metadata. This dataset includes details such as surrounding vehicles, cyclists, and pedestrians, along with situational awareness metrics. Designed to support various simulation and behavior modeling tasks, we also present the CeND-B, an open-source tool that enables users to convert raw trajectory data into comparable situational contexts.

The current global spread of the SARS-CoV-2 virus has prompted numerous countries to prioritize tracking infected individuals and their close contacts to curb transmission. While location history data has long served as a method for disease contact tracing, smartphone-generated real-time geolocations offer granular precision that significantly surpasses traditional reporting methods. This paper introduces a robust, statistically informed attack model targeting anonymous data from national contact tracing COVID-19 apps. By framing the problem within a Markov Switching Susceptible-Infected-Recovered (SIR) context and utilizing a transition matrix to simulate virus propagation, we demonstrate that this approach enhances our understanding of the attack's efficacy. Leveraging this statistical foundation, we evaluate the practical feasibility of such breaches in two prominent applications: ExpoNeTrace in Brazil and the widely adopted CoronaWatch. Our findings indicate that statistical location tracking can drastically amplify the success rate of these attacks, rendering the entire concept of anonymous data in this context effectively meaningless.

Quantum neural networks (QNNs) represent a developing field where quantum principles are integrated into the design, training, and execution of these systems. This work explores data preprocessing techniques for quantum machine learning, focusing on the field of Quantum Linear Algebra applied to machine learning. We outline various schemes for injecting machine learning data into a quantum system and examine how data can be loaded into NNs through principles of quantum linear algebra. Additionally, we evaluate the field relevance of these data preloading strategies for both practical quantum and theoretical fully quantum neural networks.

This research explores how machine learning and algebraic topology can be integrated to solve specific challenges in physics. We introduce a method based on this synthesis, which functions by training a machine to detect and learn the symmetries inherent in its data; once these symmetries are identified, they aid in resolving physics-based questions. We have applied the approach to two problem sets: (1) identifying the global symmetries of quantum field theories and theories of string through a learned central charge and other topological indicators, and (2) determining the effective field theory of string compactifications by extracting the Lie algebra of their effective global symmetries. Additionally, the work presents machine-assisted tools for formulating effective quantum field theories directly from lattice Monte Carlo simulation data.

Using the $J/\psi$ and $\eta_c$ meson pair ($e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\eta_c$) production process, we analyze the angular distributions of $J/\psi$ within next-to-leading-order (NLO) QCD calculations. Furthermore, this work incorporates charm-pomeron interactions derived from the soft theorem at both leading and next-to-leading orders to refine the analysis. Additionally, $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\chi_{cJ}$ processes are similarly scrutinized via NLO QCD frameworks and charm-pomeron channels, allowing for a comprehensive and precise numerical assessment of angular observables around the charm-bottom threshold $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV.

This paper investigates how everyday Signal participants understand end-to-end encryption and Security Identification Personal Identifiers (PINs). Drawing on data from six focus groups and 23 in-depth interviews, we analyzed participants' views regarding these features and documented their real-world experiences. Our study reveals that most users lack a detailed understanding of end-to-end encryption specifics. Regarding the PIN, however, insights vary; some comprehend it merely distinguishes their device from others, whereas others correctly understand it identifies a specific person or group. Crucially, we observed that users place greater confidence in the security offered by the PIN than by end-to-end encryption. These findings suggest that future Signal updates featuring a PIN feature should explicitly clarify its function to prevent misconceptions.

This paper introduces a novel explicit, closed-form solution for generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) within the context of cross-sectional curvature estimation for deep neural networks (CNNs). The derivation leverages a specific, novel algebraic property of Kronecker products and establishes the hierarchical curvature estimation framework (HCEF) algorithmic structure. The proposed technique achieves significant computational efficiency, reducing the per-iteration complexity from approximately $10^{14}$ to roughly $10^{12}$ floating-point operations. Furthermore, it demonstrates superior numerical stability in scenarios characterized by extremely small eigenvalues in the GGN matrix, all while maintaining high-quality performance in deep learning applications. The code for hierarchical curvature estimation framework (HCEF) implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/zhenguo/hcef.

This research examines how gender-mapping languages utilize gendering to influence lexical item representations, a foundation of human language that has rarely been explored quantitatively. We conducted the first large-scale analysis using word2vec on the first 100k most frequent words of German and French, finding that while gendering does affect some noun embeddings, its quantitative impact is surprisingly small. Furthermore, we investigated the intricate relationship between semantic and syntactic gendering, revealing that while the languages of French and German exhibit some alignment, this connection remains weak. To explain these nuances, we analyzed the influence of morphological complexity on these semantic cues. We discovered a strong correlation where gendering languages with lower morphological complexity display larger impacts of gendering on semantic embeddings. These insights advance the field by demonstrating that the interplay between syntax and semantics within embedding spaces can be carefully fine-tuned to reflect linguistic structure more accurately.

Under the assumption that an arithmetic group possesses a quasicompact Cartan model, we determine that the finite generation class number can be expressed as a product involving the Weyl group order, the cohomology boun. Object pose estimation is a critical component of computer vision, yet it remains difficult due to issues like occlusion and computational demands from large annotated datasets. Machine learning approaches depend heavily on data, typically requiring extensive label collections and often necessitating retraining when encountering new objects. This paper introduces the concept of detecting the pose for zero-shot class-level object instances, effectively decoupling object detection and pose estimation tasks. We introduce a new method grounded in the relationship between the pose of an object's category and its visual appearance, a strategy that significantly reduces the training overhead compared to traditional techniques. Furthermore, we release the "Zero-shot CLOPE" model, which requires merely 100 images per category and offers significantly flexible zero-shot class-level capabilities. We evaluate this approach using a newly developed dataset named ZCCWOPE, covering 1,008 categories. Experiments indicate that detecting the pose for a previously unseen category achieves accuracy comparable to models trained on finer-grained details using the same categories.

Accurate and efficient traffic prediction is essential for urban transportation management, public policy, and safety. However, the challenges of computational complexity and prediction errors increase with network scale and time horizons, creating a need for algorithms that are both scalable and precise. This paper proposes a novel forecasting method utilizing a deep learning framework driven by similarity, which effectively leverages similarity-based feature extraction to transform original data into components that facilitate diverse and robust machine learning model training. Validation on real-world datasets with varying sizes and forecast durations demonstrates that the proposed model significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in accuracy, and its parameters can be trained rapidly, making it highly scalable. The findings indicate that the learned feature set is not only robust and versatile but also yields superior performance when integrated into extensive traffic forecasting applications.

This study introduces VACA, a novel class of variational graph autoencoders tailored for answering interventional and counterfactual queries. The framework consists of an initial variational Bayesian conditional process that suggests latent variables based on the structure of a target system and the available evidence, as well as a subsequent sampling step used to generate predictions for interventional or counterfactual data. The method relies on the variational evidence lower bound to learn a flexible and expressive joint distribution over model parameters, latent variables, and observable variables. The authors demonstrate through empirical evaluations on three synthetic datasets and validate results with a simulation based on the Generalized Linear Model representing a tobacco use and health dataset. Additionally, the method's utility extends further to tasks such as parameter identification and prediction repair. This approach stands as a flexible Bayesian graphical framework capable of accommodating various observational and interventional data types, as well as supporting the inference of missing mechanisms and parameters.

This study presents the electro-thermal voltage and power flow dynamics inherent in modern grids integrated with inverter-based resources (IBRs). A new frequency-voltage model is formulated to capture the low-frequency oscillations caused by the electrical load's thermal time constant and inverter-based resource penetration, highlighting their potential to induce thermal overloads and thermal overvoltages. To mitigate these adverse thermal fluctuations, additional sources of frequency regulation are introduced. These auxiliary frequency services provide damping effects that prevent stability issues arising from thermal-inertia interactions. Specifically, electrothermal overvoltage phenomena are analyzed using the admittance matrix, demonstrating how local frequency-based control can avert such failures. Findings indicate that for a given IBR penetration level, there exists an optimal control strategy that minimizes the required capacity of auxiliary frequency-based control to stabilize thermal overvoltage behavior.

This paper reviews how intelligent methods, particularly machine learning, address security challenges in large-scale cyber-physical systems (CPS) composed of interconnected networks. It analyzes security issues across three dimensions: detection (identifying attacks), prevention (mitigating attacks), and response (countering active attacks), highlighting the specific role of intelligent techniques in each area. Given the complexity of managing security for extensive CPS infrastructures made of integrated components, these techniques are essential. Finally, ongoing research directions and future prospects are outlined.

We investigate the influence of three-dimensional flows on travel time measurements, specifically focusing on horizontal flows and flows associated with magnetic activity. Three-Divergence data were generated using 3D-Magneto-Convection simulations, which were then analyzed to determine their contribution to travel time changes. This study examines stochastic background signals generated by primordial electromagnetic fields (EMFs) and their interaction with the cosmic microwave background (CMB) during the CMB's emission era. We calculate the resulting stochastic gravitational wave (GW) spectra and demonstrate that the GW signal intensity increases with the EMF energy density. Notably, an EMF reaching a rough energy density of $10^{-5}$ relative to the universe could produce a GW signal potentially detectable by the Pulsar Timing Array network.

We present a new approach to compressing light field data. Unlike methods that treat each view as an isolated image, our framework acknowledges the three-dimensional arrangement of views to enable viewing from multiple points. By leveraging 3D priors, particularly depth maps, we achieve both higher quality and greater efficiency. The proposed pipeline includes a virtual camera synthesis module that projects source views onto novel target viewpoints and utilizes an advanced joint modeling strategy to improve lossless visual reconstruction despite limited bitrate constraints. Additionally, we have developed a disparity-aware model that balances rate and fidelity across multiple camera angles. Extensive tests demonstrate that our solution outperforms state-of-the-art light field compression techniques.

This study investigates a new hybrid approach combining the interactive (IRWIN) and non-interactive (CuQIR) frameworks specifically for vector-based Cross-Lingual Information Retrieval (Cross-LIX). By synthesizing these sources, the approach aims to unify the strengths of both frameworks. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses both the interactive and non-interactive baselines, confirming that the benefits of each framework can be successfully leveraged within a unified framework.

This study investigates the electronic excitations within the MA$_2$Z$_4$ family (M = Mo, W, Ti; A = Si, Ge; Z = N, P, As), utilizing first-principles electronic structure calculations to determine dielectric and optical properties. Planets are believed to form within protoplanetary disks located around young stars. While the specific formation mechanism of these disks remains uncertain, they are thought to emerge from the gravitational collapse of pre-stellar cores. In this study, we utilize numerical simulations to model the evolution of protoplanetary disks during the collapse of young stars, specifically analyzing a pre-stellar core with a mass of 0.8 solar masses and an initial radius of 1000 AU. We employ the popular Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPM) code, incorporating dust cooling, magnetic fields, magnetic transport of viscosity, and feedback from photoionizing radiation. Initially, the core collapses along a magnetic field line, forming a disk with a viscosity of around 0.01 driven by magnetic instabilities. This process results in a final core-mass of 0.28 solar masses and a disk with a maximum radius of approximately 60 AU. Furthermore, the mass of the resulting disk is highly sensitive to the core's initial mass and size, and the disk can be dispersed entirely by photoionizing radiation if the core is sufficiently massive.

We investigate the connection between leptogenesis and dark energy using a unified model grounded in string theory and the hidden sector. In this framework, dark energy density corresponds to the dilaton field, which governs the couplings for hidden sector particles. By extending the model's parameters through a superpotential derived from the Green-Schwarz mechanism, particle masses are determined. The model accommodates the observed matter asymmetry via thermal leptocenes, occurring within a high-temperature regime below the dilaton field's freeze-out. Additionally, it offers a viable explanation for the dilaton's mass and its associated cosmological evolution.

We introduce "Joint Data-Driven Control" (JDDC), a novel framework designed to simultaneously learn the structures of dynamical systems and their parameters. Our method integrates "side information"—intermediate representations of the system, such as sparsity patterns, positive constraints, or frequency band limitations—into the learning loop. This augmentation enables more efficient and rapid identification of system characteristics, particularly when training data is scarce. To validate our framework, we applied it to the challenging "Learning Flight Control with Limited Data" scenario involving a quadcopter. Remarkably, within just one trial and using only a small dataset, our method successfully generated stable flight controls. Furthermore, by imposing sparsity and positive semi-definiteness constraints, we significantly reduced the amount of data required for learning. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first instance where data-driven control techniques have been applied to achieve stable flying with such limited data and high constraints.

Neural architecture search (NAS) has become a widely used framework for automatically discovering efficient neural network structures, yet the majority of current approaches rely on surrogate models. These surrogate models estimate the performance of a new architecture based on a finite pool, where each sample is evaluated via training and then used to build the model. A primary limitation of this strategy is the interference inherent within the sample set, which arises from both functionally similar structures that share performance traits and functionally dissimilar ones that happen to overlap in performance metrics. Compliance constitutes a core component of business process management, enabling compliance engineers to define rules that ensure process instances strictly adhere to specific constraints, whether mandatory steps, prohibitions, or required actions. By identifying key mathematical concepts and their interrelationships, the method generates novel network-based features that supplement traditional dense vector representations derived from pre-trained language models. Additionally, to resolve issues related to label bias, we develop a proposal method that transforms classification into a regression task by estimating the distance of queries from decision boundaries. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating math entity association features substantially enhances classification performance across multiple tasks.

In the context of many-to-many matching, the length of the waiting period until participants are matched can significantly impact real-world applications, such as organ transplantation. To address this issue, researchers have developed various matching rules that delay the acceptance of pairing proposals to specific recipients in order to accelerate overall matches. This paper introduces a new selection mechanism for making these pairing requests. We demonstrate mathematically that our proposed rule results in shorter average waiting times compared to established methods, using both theoretical models and empirical simulations to support these findings.

Summary evaluation is critical for task alignment and quality enhancement yet remains difficult due to summaries' open-ended and subjective nature. Although human evaluation is the standard, it is resource-intensive and impractical for large-scale automated assessments to fully replace it. We present SummScore, an automated metric designed as a comprehensive assessment of summary excellence, employing a cross-encoder model pre-trained on an expanded dataset of high-quality human-written summary pairs. This study provides an in-depth analysis of SummScore's performance across multiple datasets, benchmarking it against state-of-the-art automated and existing human evaluation proxies. Crucially, we demonstrate an unprecedented strong correlation between SummScore and human judgments, establishing it as a robust metric for automated summary evaluation.

This paper establishes the existence of globally convergent gradient descent methods for both sparse and non-sparse scenarios within an explicit and well-defined range. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrate that the restored signals using this restoration algorithm exhibit significant noise resilience.

This study presents a novel theoretical framework for incompressible turbulent fluids with added heat dissipation, incorporating the influence of thermal diffusion. Our model, which extends the works of Onuki and Mikami, accounts for the role of thermal disturbance, consistent with experimental data. Our analysis of the steady turbulent state in the dissipative regime reveals that increased thermal disturbance significantly broadens the energy spectrum, a phenomenon we explain through the reduction in the effective viscosity coefficient. Additionally, our examination of the turbulent state in the presence of a temperature differential demonstrates that, in the dissipative regime, the system's energy consumption is dominated by heat transport rather than viscous loss. Our findings further confirm that the heat flux remains a non-vanishing, independent variable in the steady-state dissipative regime, a conclusion that aligns with both our theoretical predictions and the results of numerical simulations.

We offer a detailed numerical simulation of the intraliquid heat generation mechanism induced by a laser—a process crucial to understanding the complex diffraction patterns generated. A key mechanism driving this process is the light's absorption coefficient rising alongside temperature, a factor often overlooked in earlier numerical and experimental studies. This mechanism leads to a temperature-dependent variation in the refractive index gradient ($\frac{d n}{d z}$), resulting in the formation of a grating due to Brillouin scattering. This dynamic creates a feedback loop where heat generation intensifies in regions of high intensity (peaks) and decreases in regions between them. This mechanism results in the formation of two distinct patterns: one mirroring the laser beam itself and another resulting from Brillouin diffraction. This study demonstrates that this phenomenon is not merely theoretical but observable through theoretical and experimental means.

This study introduces H-STREAM, a new analytical engine designed to handle massive streams and historical datasets. H-STREAM integrates the STREAM framework for processing continuous data flows with HistGRID, a distinct storage system optimized for HISTGRID-like histogram-structured historical data. Developed as a benchmark architecture for systems facing simultaneous stream ingestion and historical data querying, H-STREAM features a benchmark engine that executes historical queries directly on continuous streams without requiring data movement. By leveraging the concept of a query plan as a functional state machine, the system allows these queries to be compiled into query histograms (Q-Histograms). These histograms represent a query as a sequence of histogram operations, enabling the system to bypass unnecessary stream evaluations and cache results. Empirical evaluations indicate that despite the query's continuous execution, historical performance dominates the response time. Consequently, the architecture delivers superior efficiency, often achieving up to tenfold performance improvements over existing streaming analytics benchmarks.

Knowledge representation and reasoning (KRR) frameworks are increasingly vital across numerous machine learning domains, such as semantic search, machine translation, and neural text generation. Knowledge-aware neural machine translation (KT), a subset of translation, enhances translation accuracy by integrating external knowledge bases (KBs) to enrich translation models. Nevertheless, managing these KBs remains a significant hurdle; specifically, a high density of entities within a KB can cause both memory and computational overloads. This issue is particularly acute for SPARQL translators, which must navigate complex queries to retrieve answers from the KB. To address these challenges, this study introduces a dual-deduplication strategy aimed at reducing the density of internal KBs. This approach retains semantic integrity and inference capabilities while improving efficiency. The methodology was validated on the SemEval-2016 NEURAL task using the Flan-T10 model, demonstrating that the deduplicated KBs achieved superior performance over those that were not processed.

The importance of a publication is typically evaluated using citation counts, which, however, show weak or inconsistent relationships with diverse metrics including new citation counts, citation speeds, and future citation predictions. A simple replacement for these future-oriented measures is the choice of venue; yet, this also fails to consistently mirror recent citation trends. Although we have demonstrated that venue-based evaluations are inherently biased due to the publication venue itself, we have shown that a citation count—adjusted to account for these venue effects—maintains a robust, significant, and significant correlation with citation-speed-adjusted venue impact. Consequently, we conclude that modified venue impact serves as a far more objective and reliable proxy for venue impact than raw venue classifications.

This work investigates a control framework designed to handle uncertainty, with a particular focus on the challenge of non-linear systems affected by modelling errors. While previous research suggests that neural networks can approximate these errors, our contribution establishes the conditions under which the accuracy of this approximation is valid. We propose a specific methodology for controlling systems within the context of neural approximation error bounds. Notably, our analysis does not rely on any assumptions regarding the rank of the perturbation. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed theory by applying it to two examples: error bounds for neural networks and a simulation of the SINS/INS integration control architecture.

This study introduces FHGO, a novel object detection and grouping method designed to handle multiple instances within specific categories. Traditional approaches typically rely on a two-stage framework: an initial object detection phase followed by a grouping stage that leverages object features, often leading to lost object overlaps within the bounding boxes and limited capacity to handle multiple instances. To address these limitations, our method utilizes a two-detector strategy to ensure the extraction of high-quality object information from within the final bounding boxes while fully supporting multi-object detection. Additionally, our dedicated grouping system leverages a graph neural network enhanced with a set-of-features attention mechanism to effectively manage multiple potential detection results. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques on both the PASCAL VOC and COCO datasets. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Cheng-Yi-Hsiao/FGHO.

Restoring visual data from incomplete information is vital for numerous real-world applications, such as recovering images from missing CT slices, MRI slices, or hyperspectral bands. This study introduces a new inverse problem framework for streaming restoration that leverages high-order tensor structures. We propose the Streaming Tensor Ring (StRR) model, which learns an implicit, high-rank update operator to map low-rank representations to the original tensor space. Specifically, StRR utilizes the tensor ring technique to monitor a small set of neighboring patches within the incoming data stream. These patch-level monitoring signals inform the reconstruction of the original high-resolution missing data. The method further supports online adaptation to non-stationary data distributions and was evaluated on synthetic reconstruction, functional stream learning, and real-world imaging modalities. Our proposed algorithm achieved state-of-the-art accuracy in all scenarios, demonstrating superior effectiveness and efficiency.

This study presents the inaugural direct demonstration that turbulent flows of inertial waves possess an energy spectrum of $E(\omega)\sim\omega^{-2/3}$, a hallmark of the Zakharov-Kolmogorov (ZK) framework. Our findings, derived from direct numerical simulations of rotating turbulence within a periodic cubic domain, align closely with theoretical predictions. Specifically, we identify parallel wavevectors oriented along a preferred axis, a signature predicted by the ZK model. Notably, contrary to predictions regarding the ZK model where this preference should be absent, we observe this alignment. Despite this discrepancy, energy spectrum predictions remain consistent. Simultaneously, we detect a preferred rotation sense in the dominant wave modes, another characteristic of the ZK model. The alignment of wavevectors vanishes upon removal of the bias in rotational sense, whereas the tendency for unidirectional wave modes disappears when preferred sense of rotation is absent. These observations confirm that both spectral behavior and wave structure emerge due to rotational bias. Our results validate ZK model applicability in rotating systems exhibiting a net rotation sense, with wave preference likely arising from finite domain size rather than helical turbulence.

The emergence of graphene has triggered significant interest in its electronic and transport characteristics. This study examines the thermodynamic, electronic, and transport properties of a regulated, electrically controlled single-layer monolayer graphene using Density Functional Theory (DFT) alongside the nonequilibrium Green's function method. Results indicate that an electric regulator enables the simultaneous manipulation of both bandgap and work function. Furthermore, horizontal application of an electric field allows for the adjustment of layer charge, thereby influencing doping. To explore the thermodynamic aspects, the Helmholtz free energy relative to layer displacement was calculated via static lattice dynamics; both in-plane and out-of-plane Free Energy trends align with prior findings from dynamic calculations. Additionally, phonon dispersion and production analyses confirmed the absence of imaginary modes, indicating structural stability. Finally, the study addresses the electronic and transport regimes by evaluating the single-layer band structure, density of states, conductance, and conductance fluctuations.

This study details the discovery of low-frequency (3.5 MHz) radio bursts from the binary system CR Dra, consisting of the M dwarf CR Dra and the K giant HD 151395. The data, gathered using the UTM Radio Telescope, reveal that HD 151395's radio activity is characterized by a spectrum of activity (SSA) exceeding 100%, driven primarily by electron cyclotron maser (EMC) emission synchronized with the system's orbital period. This emission is hypothesized to be caused by plasma within the star's wind interacting with the magnetic fields of the companion, thereby modulating the wind dynamics. Significant radio bursts were also detected from the M dwarf star CR Dra, which exhibit SSA values ranging from 10% to 100% and durations of several minutes to several hours. These specific SSA characteristics suggest a mechanism linked to the magnetosphere-ionosphere dynamics of CR Dra.

We present Articulated Neural Visualization (ANR), a new framework for rendering photorealistic humanavatars supported by articulated skeletal skeletons. Our approach employs a "Neural Skin," a learned, implicit representation that maps to 3D space based on local skeletal joint positions. This model allows us to capture human appearance from a single image recorded at a known pose, generalizing effectively to arbitrary poses, camera viewpoints, and lighting angles. Our image capture and reconstruction pipeline utilizes an image editing technique combined with iterative optimization. Specifically, fine-tuning a 3D representation involves optimizing internal representations while preserving the global parameters like scene geometry and global surface textures. We then deploy this compact neural representation for real-time rendering through differentiable volumetric techniques. Furthermore, our representation supports novel view synthesis under arbitrary coloration conditions thanks to newly introduced global basis functions. Our method has been evaluated on publicly available datasets, including the Multi-Pix and the Multi-Source datasets. Performance results show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, including the Multi-Pix dataset and the Multi-Source datasets.

The advent of deep learning algorithms has accelerated the development of image analysis tools, though human visual perception remains a critical benchmark for quality control and objective assessment. This study examines how humans and machine learning models (specifically CNNs) react to minute alterations in images, aligning with the core premise of computer vision adversarial research. We explore this topic through two primary lenses: the neurological mechanisms behind human visual perception and the performance of CNNs as artificial vision systems. Consequently, we created a novel method to assess human sensitivity to intense image modifications. Unlike previous approaches that focused on whether humans could detect changes or identified specific modifications humans could detect, this model presents a set of altered images aligned with the y-axis of classification (e.g., black-and-white for grayscale) and asks observers to identify the original, unmodified version. We evaluated human responses using low-level image alterations, such as quantization, and assessed their sensitivity across diverse image sources and grayscale levels. Our findings indicate that humans struggle to identify original images when exposed to significant adversarial perturbations, especially at lower grayscale resolutions. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to quantify human sensitivity to intense visual perturbations, and the results suggest that humans are more vulnerable to intense adversarial attacks than deep learning CNNs.

Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the topological link invariants constructed via conformal field theory methods and those resulting from $q$-analogs of the Reshetikhin-Turaev framework within the same algebra.

Our findings reveal that low-energy dynamics are characterized by two distinct timescales governed by $J$ and $J_\tau$. Although Language Models (LMs) have achieved remarkable success in language-based zero-shot learning, current approaches typically rely on specific prompts to fine-tune an LM on a limited set of pre-defined cues. In this paper, we investigate zero-shot learning by fine-tuning an LM on a collection of tasks, adapting the procedure of multi-tasking to this setting. We introduce a task-attention mechanism that dynamically influences the importance of individual tasks during the training process of each task, and we explore the use of this mechanism for zero-shot inference. Our research demonstrates that training the model on tasks spanning different taxonomies of an ontology enhances its ability to generalize to unobserved classes. Our experimental results demonstrate that training an LSTM on multiple tasks using our Task-Aware mechanism outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in few-shot and unsupervised learning scenarios by up to 10%. Our code is available at https://github.com/axel-jean/paper-code-axeljeje.

The structural, magnetic, and physical properties of the cubic intermetallic Cr2Al have been examined. Characterization involved high-resolution X-ray diffraction, measurements of lattice thermal expansion, electrical resistivity, and AC susceptibility. The unit cell was established as a face-centered cubic structure with the space group *Fm$\bar{3}$*m, where the chromium atoms occupy the 4a (0, 0, 0) sites and aluminum occupies the 16e position with parameter $z$. While magnetization data previously indicated chromium atoms at the 4a site are disordered, resistivity measurements at 2K revealed significant anomalies at 60K, suggesting the presence of additional magnetic order. Examination of the resistivity hysteresis loop at 6K further indicated the existence of domains with contrary magnetization. Consequently, it was determined that the magnetic arrangement is complex: the dominant structure follows the proposed *E*-type antiferromagnetic alignment, but the atoms at the aluminum site (magnetization of Cr atoms at the possible occupancy positions of Cr atoms at the 16e) show in-plane magnetization behavior. The interaction between Cr atoms at different positions is governed by the exchange coupling, which is the main factor in the observed behavior.

In this note, we develop a graded bosonic system to represent the invertible bosonic form of the one-dimensional Dunkl intertwining operator for zero mass. The creation and annihilation operators act on the Fock-type Hilbert space constructed from the product of the classical line and the occupation (bosonic) space, and their explicit definitions reveal the interrupt operator as a unitary map. This connection between massless Dunkl intertwining invertibility and graded bosonic systems generalizes to higher-dimensional cases involving the Fock representation of the unitary equivalence.

A nonlinear observer design method, adaptable to novel epidemic spread dynamics, is introduced for the state estimation of epidemic processes. This observer functions by non-identifying the basic reproductive number, $R_0$, and only utilizes observable metrics like total confirmed cases and deaths alongside fixed parameters, including the total population size and the reporting ratio for specific causes of death; consequently, complete initial data on infected individuals is unnecessary for its implementation. First, a mathematical dynamical system is defined, representing the interplay between epidemiological evolution and its impact on population structures. This system serves as an integral part of an observer framework, with the objective being asymptotic convergence toward the true states of the infected, suspected, and other relevant categories. This objective is achieved through Lyapunov stability analysis, allowing for an analysis of convergence rates relative to specific observer configurations and their dependency on initial values.

Predicting future entities within Knowledge Graphs (KGs) is a critical field driven by the need to work with incomplete information, a challenge that is particularly relevant for dynamic KGs used in applications like fraud detection and anomaly identification. This study focuses on predicting prospective relationships in KGs that evolve over time. We demonstrate the effectiveness of leveraging graph static structural frameworks for temporal knowledge graph forecasting. Our analysis reveals that integrating multiple instances of the same graph structure within a single model, along with employing graph augmentations, significantly enhances forecasting accuracy. To this end, we propose a novel unified architecture designed to capture various representations of a graph structure. Our experimental results across three temporal datasets, alongside an in-depth examination of a novel fraud detection use case, validate our method's strong empirical performance.

Ultrafast oscillators employing mode-locking with the Kerr-lens technique have been the standard approach for generating gigahertz repetition-rate pulses capable of reaching peak powers in the hundreds of megawatts range for decades. This consistency stems from the technique's simplicity, compactness, and practical operational characteristics. This article offers a detailed investigation of the beam profiles inherent to Kerr-l lens mode-locked oscillators, revealing cross-sectional Gaussian distributions that evolve into flat-topped shapes as diffraction effects diminish near the source. This behavior is a unique characteristic of these oscillators; in contrast, superimposed Gaussian profiles typical Fresnel cones do not appear. Furthermore, the study outlines the principles and practical applications of utilizing flat-top beams in optical manipulation contexts such as laser micro-machining and non-linear optics.

We present a method for modeling the distribution and power of nonlinear distortion in dual-polarization signals across three 4D modulation formats. This model is formulated using the modulation transfer function (MTF) derived from the model dispersion model. Experimental results affirm the model is valid, and we also provide the corresponding mathematical formulas. Visible light imaging is fundamental for wildfire detection, research, and monitoring. However, dense foliage often blocks ground fires from view due to visible wavelengths being absorbed or reflected, rendering traditional optical surveillance ineffective. Consequently, there is an urgent need for advanced methods to capture clear fire imagery regardless of vegetation density. This study introduces FIRe-GAN, a novel, foundational, unsupervised deep learning fusion method that produces synthetic visible-light fire imagery from raw thermal data, effectively decoupling fire signatures from their detection point. FIRe-GAN employs a generative adversarial network (GAN) framework; specifically, it utilizes a generator to create synthetic visible fire images from thermal inputs, while a discriminator assesses whether these outputs are indistinguishable from real photographic ground fire data. The methodology was evaluated using 865 actual terrestrial fire images and 862 corresponding thermal pairs sourced from online repositories. Results demonstrate that the generated imagery exhibits statistical equivalence to the training dataset and achieves a Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) of 1.78. Furthermore, FIRe-GAN outperforms prior state-of-the-art GAN approaches in both image fidelity and similarity metrics. Ultimately, this robust fusion technique enables the deployment of compact thermal cameras in wildfire scenarios, facilitating the creation of extensive fire imagery datasets from limited visual inputs.

Depression is a prevalent mental health issue among individuals, notably among younger generations, with social media postings often reflecting their emotions. Since users may allude to their condition directly or only indirectly, identifying these indicators can facilitate earlier diagnosis. This paper outlines the collection of a publicly available social media dataset and offers empirical evidence supporting their utility in detection algorithms. Furthermore, it identifies gaps in current research practice and dataset characteristics that can enhance the performance of machine learning models in this domain.

This study investigates how the dynamics of stick-slip systems with Coulomb resistance evolve under a feedback control mechanism designed to ensure zero steady-state error. The system's motion is modeled using linear mass-spring-damper dynamics, where the driving force is governed by a periodic sine wave, while friction resistance is defined as Coulomb friction, with the exception of a small viscous friction component. Building upon an existing sliding mode controller, we propose a new control structure that significantly restricts or eliminates velocity chattering and prevents stuck-in-place conditions during the transient phase. Furthermore, we present a theoretical proof that the closed-loop system is finite-time semi-global stable, converging to zero velocity and acceleration. Our experimental results, derived from tests on an electro-mechanical setup, confirm the effectiveness of the proposed strategy.

Although agent optimization under model misspecification is well-established theoretically, it remains largely unexplored within the scope of Hedging problems. To address this, we introduce a novel variant termed "Bellman Hedging," which applies optimization principles to such scenarios. Theoretically, we demonstrate that while convergence to equilibrium is not assured, the algorithm yields suboptimal values diminishing at a sublinear rate. By establishing robust links between Bellman Hedging and Profound Belman Q-learning, we prove that a logarithmic number of failures—instances where hedging losses are not sufficiently improved—is achievable. We also show that the approach remains stable within noisy environments, delivering an optimal linear rate for Bellman Q-learning even when estimates are subject to disturbances. Finally, we confirm the method's efficacy empirically across numerous scenarios involving model misspecification, including cases where data is corrupted by errors.

Sequential recommenders, which predict the next item a user will select based on their item interaction history, are extensively utilized in real-world applications. Nevertheless, most existing approaches focus solely on discerning the motivation driving that specific hidden propensity, leaving motivation models ineffective when the relevant features are sparse or ambiguous. Consequently, these systems often fail to integrate seamlessly with other components essential for enhancing overall performance and to integrate complementary signals, such as historical interaction data. This paper introduces a hidden user motivation modeling architecture specifically designed for sequential recommenders. By leveraging a hidden interest representation for each user, which is trained via a hidden motivation representation using a contrastive loss, we enable more effective integration of additional features. These signals can be directly fed into the primary recommender to boost performance without compromising the interpretability of the model's core structure. Empirical validation across three real-world datasets reveals that our approach significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in effectiveness. Furthermore, when fused with other signals within a comprehensive recommender framework, our model substantially enhances their overall performance.

This research introduces a decentralized control framework designed to enhance both performance and robustness in multisensor and multi-channel systems. The methodology utilizes a centralized, convex optimization scheme to calculate optimal weights for individual decentralized controllers, which are then assigned to specific nodes. A key innovation is a new distributed, convex penalty term added to a standard H-infinity objective. This penalty quantifies the system's vulnerability to specific unstable poles in the open-loop transfer matrix, encouraging the regulation law to drive these entries toward zero. The resulting algorithm is distributed and enables autonomous regulation in a "plug-and-play" manner; adding or removing nodes does not necessitate recalculating regulations for the rest of the network. Furthermore, this strategy is applicable to both continuous and discrete-time domains.

Building robust large-scale AI systems requires addressing susceptibility to adversarial examples, yet their impact on speech self-supervised learning (SSL) remains poorly understood. This work provides an initial investigation into the vulnerability of SSL representations, specifically examining how factors such as corruption methods, pre-training data volume, mask parameters, and model architecture influence resistance to attacks. This work introduces a sensitivity analysis approach for missing data that leverages the E-value, a concept from robustness and causal inference that quantifies the maximum correlation between an outcome and unobserved factors, assuming those factors explain the greatest proportion of variance in the observed covariate. We apply the concept to settings with missing completely at random (MCAR), uninformative, and sensitive (S) covariates, utilizing the latter scenario for our examination. We demonstrate how the E-value establishes an upper bound for the proportion of outcome variability attributable to these unobserved factors and use it to define a plausibility threshold for the observed covariate's relevance. To test the reliability of predictions based on such information, we develop a Bayesian framework for determining the credible probability that the observed covariate is associated with the outcome under the specified sensitivity constraints. The findings reveal that the proportion of variance explained by the observed covariate is notably low, yet the likelihood of the observed outcome being predictive remains high.

By categorizing and analyzing these specific weaknesses, we aim to warn developers against similar mistakes and encourage the avoidance of unsecured custom solutions in favor of secure, established open standards.

Leveraging neural networks, automatic labeling has proven effective and cost-efficient for numerous city tasks, yet the scarcity of expert-annotated data remains a significant hurdle. To mitigate this, prior research has explored data augmentation through neural inference—generating labels for unlabeled images by training models to annotate directly. However, these earlier methods relied on neural *classification* to determine the class of an object, a process prone to errors, particularly for ambiguous instances like occluded objects. We introduce VALUE (Voting-based extensive Annotation for Urban environments via Learning), which replaces classification with neural regression to enable precise, continuous coordinate prediction. Unlike the discrete classes of prior systems, regressed coordinates are more accurate. To further enhance precision, VALUE incorporates an attentional voting mechanism that aggregates predictions from multiple samples, effectively filtering out anomalies and focusing on consistent outputs. Quick Sinkhorn II leverages the inherent structure of the optimal transport map under these specific conditions to execute the computation in linear time. Furthermore, it requires only minimal, essentially negligible preprocessing. We have established that the algorithm achieves both speed and accuracy by identifying the specific structure within the unnormalized optimal transport map derived from Sinkhorn iterations. Crucially, it refines the mapping process by utilizing the properties of the relevant sinkning matrices to perform computations in strictly linear time. Quick Sinkhorn II is designed to deliver a precise and highly efficient solution for specific optimal transport challenges, incorporating unique algorithmic enhancements that capitalize on the structural properties of the transport map to ensure rapid execution. By integrating the advantages of earlier approaches with novel optimizations targeting the cost matrix, it guarantees accurate outcomes without the overhead of extensive initial data preparation.

This study presents FUV observations of the active M dwarf star, AU Mic, obtained by the Cosmic Origins Evolutionary Spectrograph (COS) on the Hubble Space Telescope, alongside existing UV data from the International Ultraviolet Explorer (IUE). The study aims to constrain the frequency and characteristics of UV flux eruptions and determine their correlation with optical flares. Our results indicate that these eruptions occur with a mean recurrence interval of 2.2 days and exhibit no significant correlation with optical flares. Additionally, we analyze archival HST data from 2000 and 2010, revealing that UV flux eruptions remain constant over this decade. These findings suggest that stellar activity cycles in the near-UV range operate on timescales of at least ten years. By examining the timing of egress for both exoplanets AU Mic b and c, we infer that their orbits are non-transiting. Consequently, we estimate that planetary wind interactions generate stellar activity at a frequency of 2.3 days, potentially explaining the distinct variations in egress depths and profiles observed during transits.

We investigate the motion of a heavy particle traversing a medium where electrically neutral particles exhibit resistive behavior upon interaction with charged matter, a medium that decelerates charged particles through the continuous emission of radiation. A dynamic framework is established linking this acceleration to the cumulative radiation power emitted, analogous to Bateman equations in the context of classical electrodynamics. This classical system models a neutral substance similar to radiation-quark plasma; however, unlike the theoretical quark medium, real-world equivalents would be ordinary matter. Given that the intensity of this radiation-dependent drag far exceeds the standard drag force arising from virtual quantum fluctuations, we propose an analytical expression for radiative reaction forces acting on both radiating electrons and quarks. These findings hold relevance for the design of advanced radiation shields.

In machine learning, the K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) approach stands out as a straightforward yet effective tool for classification and regression. However, its accuracy often degrades significantly when confronted with imbalanced datasets. In such scenarios, the performance of KNN is typically dominated by the immanent majority class, while the significant minority class remains effectively ignored. This paper proposes a novel, statistically grounded method to address this imbalance without altering the classification process. By applying a statistical test to the feature vectors, we compute a closeness metric between data points. Crucially, this measure diverges from traditional distance calculations by differentiating between majority and minority classes, rather than relying on the uniform distances used in standard KNN algorithms. Extensive testing on imbalanced sets of varying proportions, across multiple runs and feature dimensions, demonstrates this method's superior accuracy compared to conventional KNN. The demonstrated effectiveness of this straightforward technique is particularly promising when applied to real-world domains, such as fraud detection and disease diagnosis, where identifying instances within the imbalanced class is of paramount importance.

This work introduces a framework designed to analyze and manage networked processes using only data. We begin by defining the key characteristics of such processes, emphasizing their reliance on specific topologies and the propagation of both positive and negative influences. We then establish the core principles of an image-based methodology, which models the evolution of these networks through a multidimensional, time-varying vector. Utilizing principles from control and dynamical systems theory, we develop an image-based control system capable of both predicting and shaping the process. Furthermore, we apply this methodology to $sIS$ epidemic models, presenting a method for predicting disease spread and implementing control strategies, all while requiring solely knowledge of the process history. Consequently, this data-centric strategy eliminates the need for specific parametric forms or the explicit identification of networks, which are typically difficult to obtain.

This paper examines the instability within a thin liquid layer coating a solid cylinder, specifically investigating scenarios where slip length exceeds capillary lengths. These insights advance the understanding of capillary phenomena on fibers, with significant implications for applications such as electrospinning, 3D bioprinting, and microfiber-based desalination.

Although speech recognition systems have reached high accuracy, their performance degrades significantly when exposed to out-of-distribution data, such as target sentences that differ in duration from the training set. This paper presents a proposed solution to this challenge. The method generates synthetic audio by matching sentence lengths through a non-statistical approach, eliminating the statistical inaccuracies inherent in prior deep learning-based techniques. Performance is evaluated on two corpora: Read English (Child Developmental) and shorter versions of the Google Speech Commands dataset. Results confirm that the proposed approach is effective in both settings. Finally, a comparison against current statistical and deep learning methods is provided to demonstrate the system's superiority.

This study introduces a new model designed to detect hate speech in offensive texts using advanced NLP techniques and deep learning. Its primary innovation centers on a multi-orientation framework that targets user profiles generating hate speech, specifically by integrating the application of N-Grams and a Natural Language Inference task to transform text into set structures. To further enhance performance, the model employs a pre-trained language model on transformed inputs to derive contextual representations and applies an advanced data augmentation method called Prompting for generating additional negative samples. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach surpasses current state-of-the-art solutions on all three datasets of the HSODC challenge, achieving record-breaking scores. The source code for the model will be made public to support open access.

This study introduces a Multi-input Multi-output (MIMO) architecture designed to handle both global context and local details, specifically addressing the limitation of previous approaches, such as Path Aggregation, which share features only global features. Instead, the proposed Phased Feature Sharing (PFS) module selectively exchanges local and global features based on specific thresholds. This mechanism ensures an adaptive balance between computational efficiency and performance. Additionally, the PFS module is designed to be lightweight, enabling efficient implementation. Validation through various deep learning models demonstrates that PFS significantly improves both metrics compared to Path Aggregation, achieving substantial performance gains and higher efficiency in terms of reduced parameters and fewer operations.

Historical record images serve as vital sources for comprehending the evolution of writing systems, artistic styles, and civilizations. Analyzing these records often demands sustained human effort, yet automated processing offers a more efficient alternative. To support processing in historical tasks, researchers have created numerous specialized datasets. This article provides a comprehensive review of existing datasets for historical documents and related records. It categorizes these resources into three groups based on script characteristics: (1) ancient records that predate writing system formation, (2 records featuring scripts before their standardization, and (3) records representing established and standardized forms. For each dataset, key attributes such as content, construction processes, and metadata are elaborated. Additionally, relevant image preprocessing techniques and task-specific classification algorithms are critically reviewed. Finally, the article identifies current limitations and proposes potential directions for future research in this area.

We explore the extension of twistor-creating constructions developed within chirally restricted self-dual Yang-Mills theories to higher-spin theories. Our approach utilizes the Vortex equations—specifically the ADHM correspondence—which link these to vector bundles on the projective three-space $\mathbb{CP}^3$. Although deep learning has achieved significant success in medical image analysis, acquiring annotated data remains difficult and expensive. In an effort to harness vast amounts of unlabeled data from open-source repositories, this work introduces the Label Renovation Mechanism (LRM), the first fully Bayesian approach designed to mitigate noise in medical image classification. Unlike the original labeling sources, the LRM generates clean synthetic labels by synergistically combining self-attention and convolutional operations. By applying LRMs to two publicly available datasets for pulmonary nodule classification and skin lesion categorization, the LRM achieved superior accuracy and robustness compared to conventional strategies.

Spin-polarized photon pairs have been previously established as essential resources for quantum information processing, and this work introduces a novel hybrid optical antenna, hybridizing dielectric and plasmonic components, to enhance performance. This configuration enables spin-polarized emission efficiency, luminosity, and forward-directed, highly unidirectional light to reach unprecedented levels. The dielectric antenna's dimensions are precisely tuned to maximize spin-polarization by amplifying in-plane electric fields, which interact optimally with spin-stimulated sources. Meanwhile, plasmonic structures are designed to direct most photons forward, ensuring highly efficient and parallel light propagation in a single direction. This strategy achieves an exceptionally high spin-polarization value ($P_A \approx 0.95$) and near-perfect emission efficiency ($Q \approx 0.99$). Significantly, the hybrid design also yields a previously unattained high angular polarization ($|P| \approx 0.97$), thereby facilitating compact spin-qip (quantum processing) units based on stimulated single-photon emission that are capable of generating multiple identical spin states.

We introduce a new framework designed to describe the screening of contacts within and the evolution of force chains in granular materials. Drawing inspiration from the electromagnetic screening mechanism found in plasma physics, our theory posits that particle screening and the propagation of stress chains are fundamentally governed by the balance between the local stress deviator and effective particle friction. Contrasting with previous theories that relied on global stress metrics such as anisotropy, our approach utilizes this local balancing act between frictional forces and stress deviator. Validated through computational simulations and physical experiments, the theory accurately predicts the size, intensity, and frequency of force chains. Additionally, it explains the specific conditions under which these stress chains form, break, and evolve. By employing a framework rooted in electromagnetic screening, our work establishes new pathways for investigating the collective dynamics of granular systems.

First-principle electronic structure calculations were employed to examine the interaction between silicon-based 2D material (silicene) and a hexagonal boron nitride substrate, focusing on the incorporation of monovalent manganese impurities. Our findings indicate that the $sp^2$ hybridized electronic states of silicene are modified by Mn doping. Furthermore, the system exhibits ferromagnetic ordering due to strong exchange coupling between localized $3d$ spins of Mn and delocalized $sp^2$ hybridized electrons. The arrangement of $3d$ electron spins generates a half-metallic band structure characterized by anisotropy energy of approximately $2.8 \times 10^5$ J/m$^3$. Consequently, this two-dimensional heterostructure presents significant potential for spintronic and magnetic memory technologies.

Imbalance in data across multiple classes presents a significant challenge in supervised machine learning, particularly in resource-constrained environments where obtaining further data is costly. This paper presents the development of a multi-class text categorization system, specifically targeting spam detection across 11 distinct categories. To address class imbalance in this context, the study evaluates three augmentation over-sampling methods: GAN-based, Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE), and Adaptive Undersampling Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (AUTOSTIN). The research further analyzes how these techniques perform relative to one another in handling multi-class imbalance and assesses their impact on system accuracy. Results indicate that the GAN-based over-sampling method offers a superior solution for improving multi-classification systems impacted by data imbalance.

This study investigates the interconnectedness between COVID-1 news coverage, public awareness, and audience metrics. We analyze data from KRGLO, Inc., a regional news provider catering to North Central Texas, alongside content from Yahoo! News. Our findings indicate a tight correlation between KRGLO, Inc. reporting and audience engagement, as well as consistent alignment between KRGLO, Inc. and Yahoo! outlets. However, despite expectations, the relationship between news coverage and both COVID-1 cases and deaths remains inconsistent. We further explore coverage patterns, including the timing, frequency, and depth of reporting, as well as the prominence assigned to the virus. The research also details how audience metrics—such as viewer engagement, reader volume, and ad revenue—respond to these developments.

We present preservation strategies for the total and its components of orbital angular momentum within the Rapid Multipole Method (RPM), employing the minimal coupling Hamiltonian. While the full total angular momentum can be efficiently maintained in RPM through a multipole expansion in either a spherical or multipole-preserving basis, the individual angular momentum associated with individual subshells cannot, due to the non-conservation nature of this approach. Specifically, our method allows the user to choose between conserving either the scalar product of total angular momentum and a fixed spatial vector, or the projection of that vector along the z-axis. We have evaluated the efficacy of these techniques in atoms subjected to intense, linearly or circularly polarized laser pulses, with particular attention to heavy atoms like bismuth where spin-orbit interactions are significant. Our findings indicate that the rapid multipole method, when adapted with these modifications, can reliably conserve angular momentum with high precision, regardless of whether spin-orbit coupling is included, and does so with minimal additional computational overhead.

Data collection is often the primary bottleneck in numerous machine learning applications. This paper examines a specific scenario where an interaction between a learner and an oracle occurs under the constraint that the total number of queries is strictly limited. We analyze data strategies that integrate the oracle with external data amplification techniques, specifically data augmentation, to effectively utilize information gained from each query.

We establish the capacity for interactive learner-oracle processes to achieve near-optimal performance by implementing an "amplified" approach. This method combines each query to the oracle with independent, non-interactive training on copies of that query. We further introduce the concept of "manifold structures" to model scenarios where an learner directly observes data rather than querying authorities. In these cases, we demonstrate that a similar interaction between direct observation training and query-based augmentation can achieve optimal results.

In conclusion, our findings offer practical insights into how to efficiently exploit finite-query access to oracles within machine learning. These results suggest how to boost the utility derived from every piece of information obtained, thereby addressing challenges related to data scarcity.

Detecting dark matter via the nuclear recoil signals it produces in underground experiments remains a primary objective for physics research. Among the various gas-based detection methods developed over the last few decades, the Time Projection Chamber (TPC) is the most prevalent design. Recently, advances in high-resolution, fast, and efficient gas detectors have spurred interest in using TPCs to observe dark matter nuclear recoils. This paper examines key observables that can be measured using high-performance gas TPCs to identify these events. We propose that state-of-the-art gas detectors could enable the separation of dark matter nuclear recoils from the inevitable background from neutrons within the range of interest, specifically for a target mass of 100 g and exposure times exceeding 10² g·yr. This separation is achievable even when the experiment is sensitive to dark matter cross-sections as low as 10⁻⁴⁶ cm². The key observables discussed include the number of electron holes (ionization), the time distribution of these charges (time profile), their diffusion behavior (diffusion pattern), and the pulse shape of the induced electrical signals.

A primary challenge in evaluating machine learning models lies in aligning them with both human expert judgment and legislative standards. Since experts frequently possess nuanced insights that legislation fails to articulate explicitly, regulations are often applied inconsistently when enforced without direct human involvement. To demonstrate this discrepancy, this paper examines automated driving evaluations, where experts determine success or failure based on automated system decisions rather than automated systems themselves. Our findings reveal that, according to human raters, experts penalize specific scenarios more harshly than regulations require. Consequently, we propose a novel evaluation framework that integrates contextual information to align algorithmic assessment with human expert supervision.

Since 2016, the NLP research community has been engaged in a "challenging reports" competition, where groups are tasked with creating rigorous tests that expose the limitations of In-context Learning (ICL) in current natural language processing. This technical report details the findings from the 2023 "Out-of-Context Challenge," a competition designed to assess a model's resilience when prompted with false world knowledge that contradicts reality. Participants were given three distinct tasks involving fake information: identifying a specific entity mentioned nowhere else in the prompt, extracting a specified entity despite conflicting background text, and writing a response to a query based on inconsistent context. For each task, a standardized input format was established, featuring a declaration block outlining fictional world knowledge and a subsequent task instruction. Models responded using free-text generations, with strict criteria established to automatically score outputs. Results indicate that GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 successfully utilized real-world knowledge to override contradictory information provided in prompts, achieving near-perfect performance across all three scenarios. In contrast, open-source alternatives, including PaLM 2 and various smaller variants derived from Llama 2 and Bloom, failed to ignore the deceptive context effectively, yielding poor performance. Although these underperforming models demonstrated some ability to rely on external knowledge, their success rates remained significantly below chance levels.

Geodesics serve as fundamental elements in Riemannian geometry, representing the shortest paths within a manifold. In this study, we investigate geodesics that exist inside the intrinsic manifolds of various stochastic fields. Our results demonstrate that the equations of motion for a specific manifold depend exclusively on that manifold's metric, not on its dynamics. Specifically, for Gaussian fields, we derive the fundamental metric tensors. Subsequently, we derive the corresponding equations of motion and solve them for specific cases. In addition, we present a simplified method to test a manifold for isotropy. By utilizing intrinsic metrics derived from the stochastic properties, we illustrate that the manifold of an isotropic stochastic field is itself isotropic, provided the field exhibits both spatial isotropy and homogeneity.

The STAR collaboration analyzed the directed flow ($v_1$ versus gradient) within Au+Au and isobar collisions, examining the momentum dependence of $v_1$ across an extensive range of transverse momenta. The study highlights a distinct crossover in the sign of $v_1$ for mid-rapidity regions, occurring at approximately $p_\textrm{T} \approx 1$–2 GeV/$c$. This inflection point, which coincides with the transition from the initial compression phase to the late-stage rotation of angular momentum in the collision zone, is linked to the phase diagram's critical point and potentially demarcates the transition from quark-gluon plasma to hadronic matter. We introduce a novel adaptive spectral Koopman operator-based control strategy designed for the decentralized monitoring and management of large-scale systems. Leveraging the fact that the Koopman operator is isometric on $L^2$ and can linearize nonlinear dynamics through its eigenfunctions, the methodology approximates these operators using the Goss method with rigorous error bounds. Unlike prior empirical approaches, our use of the Goss polynomial hierarchy within a Koopman framework guarantees that modeling errors decrease exponentially as the degree of the resulting linear controllers increases. Furthermore, the framework employs a new algorithm to construct an optimal polynomial basis set derived from the Goss hierarchy by utilizing a cost-based measure of dependency among observables. The efficacy of both our algorithm and the overall control method is demonstrated through a benchmark analysis involving a large-scale fluid flow simulation.
